title: Was wanting more...
text:
I can't help but feel disappointed with this game. I was hoping for something unique, but what I found was another gear based questing/dungeon/PVP game. SWTOR's biggest new advancement is full voice acting. That is a cool new feature, for a while. But, I found it bored pretty quickly. I still think it's a great new addition to the MMO genre, but it did start to get old. I truely felt underwhelmed. This is the only MMO I've played so far that didn't meet my expectations.

I suppose what I was looking for was the gear based questing/dungeon/PVP WoW model with some sandbox elements. My first MMO was Star Wars Galaxies. You had a huge amount of freedom in that game. SWTOR is very linear and confining. There isn't much to do in the game other than quests/dungeons/PVP. I stumbled into an auditorium, and I was thinking, "Cool, players can make shows and have weddings here.". But, you can't even sit in the chairs. Why even make an auditorium and not allow players to sit down to enjoy some player created content?

There is currently no player housing. I knew people in SWG that redecorated their houses every few weeks. It was a big deal to some people. You could orient items however you liked, and people were so creative. I remember walking into a house and they had taken boulders and made it look like a cave. I was blown away. We use to have block parties, weddings and fashion shows, ext. We use to have guild wars and could set up turrets to help defend the town. You could craft in your house, then put them up for auction while still in your house with vendors that you set up.

I haven't seen any cosmetic clothing yet. Maybe I just haven't leveled high enough, but I haven't seen it yet. For role players, this is kind of a big deal. Sometimes it was an achievement like getting a full set of stormtrooper armor and a carbine so you could walk around feeling like a stormtrooper. Even people like me who don't role play enjoy having something different to wear to distinguish you from the crowd. In WoW, once I got my raid set, that was about it.

The character and race selection is horrible. I didn't find only having four body types to be that big of a deal. But, I didn't like the hairstyles at all. And, the little extras like tattoos or horns were all so similar you really couldn't distinguish yourself. And, all the races were human. No Wookies, Rodians, ext. It just feels so confining.

So what's the big deal about role playing or sandbox elements? I worry that the community will become what WoW's community has become. A bunch of kids or elitist punks. I've been playing LOTRO the past few months, and I don't think I've heard the word "noob" or "pwned" once. It's kind of like the difference between going to a fine dinning restaurant and your local McDonalds. You don't find a lot of screaming kids in a fine dinning restaurant. If you want a more mature playerbase, then you have to give them the tools to do other things than obsess on gear and who's 1337.

The graphics weren't great, but I was expecting that. They aren't bad either. I can't say they were disappointing to me because they were about where I expected them to be. Not everyone has a maxed out system after all. I once bought a laptop and couldn't get it to play WoW. I had to return it and get an upgraded model. So, I know they were trying to get the maximum amount of people whose systems could handle it. I can't fault them on that.

Ambient sounds are missing from the game. And I've heard very little of the original soundtrack. Playing Star Wars Galaxies and hearing the original soundtrack really made me feel like I was in the Star Wars universe, and I was missing that in this game. I guess I kinda miss the whole timeline from the movies as well. I miss seeing stormtroopers and AT-AT's and the like. I just didn't feel immersed in the Star Wars universe that I know and love. It's someone elses Star Wars universe, not the one I grew up with.

Not sure still if I like the group questing in dungeons (flashpoints). Did one with a person that was lagging pretty bad, and we constantly had to wait for him because you all have to talk to the NPC to get quest dialog at the same time. It made for a terribly long and boring dungeon. We could have talked to the NPC and cleared trash while he caught up if we weren't all required to talk at the same time.

The space combat is just a mini game. I think I saw that they may add a more robust space aspect to this game in the future. Which is fine, Star Wars Galaxies didn't launch with a space feature at all. But, if it is going to remain as just something to kill time, that would be very disappointing. Space is a huge part of Star Wars. If I wanted to play a mini game I would sit down and play a hand of Sabaac with another player...if I could sit down. I hope this gets addressed soon in a meaningful way.

Don't get me wrong, I enjoy questing and dungeons and PVP. I just want....more. I am the type of person that tries to complete every quest, even if they are grey. Most of the things I mentioned like sitting down in chairs, player cities and bases and cosmetic clothing are simply tools and really wouldn't effect the gameplay at all. And, they still may add them in later. But, I don't want to be dragged along for years hoping they'll add them, and they never do. I think I'm going to wait a few months to see what direction they are going in before I put down money on a monthly subscription.

title: Playable and time consuming, but not special
text:
This is a game that can definitely burn a number of hours as you build up forces and try to conquer the world. In style of play it most resembles Elemental or Civ V than other older turn-based 4X games.

I have to say that I liked elemenats of hte game, but could not call this a masterpiece. The standard for most fantasy 4X games is still Master of Magic. Yes, the graphics are terrible, but the shear number of races and spells and the addition of heroes made the game a huge step up compared to the other options. Age of Wonders tries to capture the same elements, but for me it never quite achieved the same elegance.

Warlock doesn't try to be as expansive as Master of Magic. There are only 3 races and no technology tree. The only research is for spells, and the research tree is rather linear, you see 5 options to research and from what I could see the system works by a "researched X spell and spell X+1 appears in the tree. The spells appear to follow a very linear tech tree.

Combat is not much different than Civ V, the lack of stacking makes it a bit more tactically than Civ IV, but it's still rather straightforward in execution.

Honestly, this feels like it could have been a lot better if more time had been spent expanding options. The lack of races, the lack of a tech tree, the linear nature of spell research, all leaft me thinking the game could be so much more.

But I love 4X games, so I still enjoy this one. It plays faster and smoother than Elemental, and while lacking in some elements, does not have the same balance issues that make Elemental nearly impossible to enjoy.

If you like 4X games, and like the idea of adding magic, this is worth trying. Otherwise, it will likely frustrate you.

Bad:

*Multiplayer as of when this review was written, is hacker infested. Even Crytek is aware of this. I've had more fun playing the original's multiplayer than this game, even though I was never good in Crysis Wars.

Overall: Crysis 2 reeks of console part, right from opening menu, all the way through its unoriginal gameplay. This what happens when developers try way too hard to compete with the Call of Duty series. It has to stop.

title: Oh, my achin' agin' anteriors!!
text:
Santa dropped this off at our house the other day, and I'm pretty sure he had a smile on his ruddy face when he did it. "I'll teach those bleedin' couch potatoes", he said with a laugh. "Ho Ho Ho", and off the old jelly belly flew, with his sleigh full of Wii related accoutrements for sedentary families around the world.

Having the good fortune to have a semi-geek in the house, the Wii thing was soon set up in the kid's bedroom, and after 5 hours I thought I should check on the adult kid and the little kid - just in case.

Santa had sadistically included an extra controller and nunchuk with the package, so added to the pair that comes with the set, a full scale 2 kid war was in progress, covering bragging rights for five included games - boxing (little kid leading), bowling (big kid ahead), baseball (no clear advantage - but then we don't play baseball here, because it's just not cricket), tennis (neither will see Wimbledon) and golf (Tiger's safe for now)

They had set up a Mii (avatar) for each member of the family (self included), and looking at the body shape they chose for me, I immediately remembered that I should make a New Year resolution to lose weight.

Soon enough a challenge was issued, and hours later I emerged as the household bowling champion, but threatening to sue for physical abuse for my boxing loss. (I think they made it personal)

All these games have an aerobic and physical element, and if you don't get yer lazy azz in gear, nothing much happens. Bowling for instance, requires you to swing the controller like you would a bowling ball (making sure that you secure it around your wrist first so you don't put a hole in your TV), and after hours of unaccustomed exercise, your muscles can really feel the burn. And it's not only your arm muscles. One does not bowl without the correct body language after all.

Oh the pain!!

Now they're looking at all the other doo-dads and wing-dings to further their Wii experience, and making strong birthday and father's day hints. IMHO they should drop off their requests to the fat man in the red suit, and get HIM to come over and play some games.

Off to review some Icy Hot and Radian B, and make a massage appointment.

Amanda Richards, December 28, 2008

title: Return to PopoloCrois
text:
I've played Harvest Moon games, now generally known as Story of Seasons, but I've not heard of PopoloCrois before, but that's not affecting my game play. If I were to compare this with anything, I'd undoubtedly say this is a bit like Rune Factory, which takes a core RPG and adds a bit of Harvest Moon features. This is heavily story-driven and the farming aspects are sorta taking backseat to everything else. It's also very slow starting, so be prepared to invest some time before you get into full swing. Even at 5 hours play time, I've not fully unlocked everything, and I'm trying to keep myself from looking up spoilers so I don't quite know how long the game is. But being one of the rare types of newer games that included a full-color manual, I know that I've still unlock StreetPass.

The game is probably pretty niche and there's nothing wrong with that. For myself, I find myself feeling a bit blasé about recent big-name releases, so this is a refreshing change of pace. There's not a cast of thousands, characters whose names I can't remember or even care about. It's not epic. It has nice colors and music, a handful of quirky characters (so far), and an overall feeling of classic JRPG game play. I keep saying "so far" or "right now", since I don't know how the game progresses, but 'right now" I have a four-member party who are searching for some number of dungeons to clear so I can progress. Movement is visually similar to classic JRPGs, with an isometric view of with your characters travelling the world and having random encounters. That's where I shudder; I guess games like Pokemon or the older, classic Final Fantasy games have given me an aversion over random encounters. You can adjust the rate, but I still have it set at the highest (which I think was the default).

Combat is decidedly JRPG: an off-world zone with a grid pattern and turn-based combat. You can toggle auto-combat or manual combat, and I've been running mostly on auto with no real problems. If I'm annoyed by the high rate of random encounters, I turn it to manual combat and select "run", but you can lose gold if you run from an encounter.

Well, I won't go on, but if you want something that's pretty stress-free, that won't cause you to rage-quit or tempt you to throw your 3DS against a wall, this is a very nice change of pace.

title: FIFA has a different feel this year
text:
Finally the champions league is in FIFA! I think this has to be my favorite addition because while you could previously play in cup tournaments or create your own tournament hearing the theme and seeing champions league in a FIFA game just feels different and long overdue.
Now onto the gameplay and this year FIFA feels intentionally slower. There have been some
New mechanics added to the game and
Thus far I am not a big fan of the 50/50 system as it seems random as opposed to skill or rating based. I would say the user loses the vast majority of the battles no matter what player you are using in my playtime so far. Speaking of which the attributes too often feel useless. If I play a through ball to an attacker making a run with a higher sprint rating in open space and they are beyond the much slower defender then the defender should not catch them as often as they do. I understand that they slowed down the whole game for the sake of "reality" however a fundamental element of the game (real and video) is making intelligent runs that expose the defense with a well timed pass. This year feels slower and I am sure those who are excellent with some of the newer trick pass animations and shots will excel but overall it makes the game feel a bit less fluid to me. I like the addition of more physicality in the game but I don't believe the balance is quite right. I also think the change in the passing mechanics so that they are less accurate is a huge mistake as far too often and randomly simple passes like through balls to open teammates or switches to the opposite side of the pitch go awry even when you are using the best passers in the game. It's still a video game and I expect precision not to mention if you watch most of the major leagues around the world the amount of basic passes that go awry without defensive intervention is minimal. I do like the new active touch system which is fun especially on volleys but it will take some more time to truly master.
The graphics from the players to the stadiums and the pitch continue to look great. The commentary also is strong with the addition of Lee Dixon and Derek Rae for the Champions league matches.
The journey mode which I enjoy is supposed to represent the end of our time with Alex Hunter. I have not finished it yet but am enjoying the use of the champions league as a focus this year. I also like the ability to play as Kim and Danny a bit more this year. I do wish there were more consequences to choices you make and branching paths that change your story but hopefully this will happen in future iterations as it would also give the mode more replay value if they hade more endings (like the surprisingly fun multi ending game Late Shift). Hopefully I can update this review once I finish the journey.

Ultimate team is the cash cow so as usual it has a ton in it and can be addictive but the best method for advancing still feels like buying as many packs as humanly possible which admittedly makes it less appealing.

I am enjoying the game despite some of its flaws but right now I would probably say it's maybe 7.5 /10.

title: Worst remote ever
text:
This is quite possibly the worst remote I’ve ever used. If you think of any problems with remotes you’ve had in the past, this one has somehow managed to include every one of them.
1. The remote has to be pointed with laser accuracy at the front of the Xbox to work. If you are pointing a bit high or low, or if there is anything blocking the beam (like a coffee table) you can forget it.
2. The main button you’ll be using is the directional pad to navigate around the Xbox menu. This button is recessed into the remote and requires a great deal of force to make it click. As a result, if you use your thumb, half of your finger will be squished painfully on the the hard remote surface. If you switch to a smaller finger like your index finger it barely fits but the force and strange angles needed to get it to work gives you arthritis like pain after a short search through Netflix.
The other buttons are very small and hard to find especially the much-needed back button.

title: Much Like the First, but Still Fun
text: I really enjoyed the first Lost Cases of Sherlock Holmes, so I bought the second one as soon as it was released.  I was not disappointed, and I enjoyed this game just as much as the first.  The gameplay and style are exactly the same as the first game, but the sequel offers new cases.  For those unfamiliar with the series, this is primarily a hidden object game, punctuated by logic-style puzzles at the end of each chapter.  The game features a series of Sherlock Holmes cases, and you must search a variety of locations to find clues to solve the mystery.  Each location reveals a number of potential suspects, and the conclusion involves solving a logic and memory puzzle to determine which party is guilty.  The cases are well-written, and the hidden object scenes are appropriate to the time and place in question (late-19th c. London).  The suspects are believable, and the objects one must find to discover suspects are appropriate to the story (perfume bottles for the mistress of a prominent politician, for example).  Those who enjoyed the first game will certainly want to play the second.  Don't expect innovation, just more of what made the first game fun.  This is definitely one of the more fulfilling hidden object games I've played recently.

title: Great clothing pack!
text:
The Diesel Stuff Pack (SP) is an add-on for the Sims 3, which means you must have the base game to run it. The DVD works on both Macs and PCs. It features a bunch of adult clothes and some objects, all from the international clothing company Diesel. Mostly I bought it because I wanted more options for my adult male Sims, and that is exactly what I got.

I didn't get this SP when it first came out because I thought it was all hipster stuff. But it really isn't hipster at all. There are way more clothes in it than I even thought there'd be, and the men's clothes are of much higher quality than one normally sees in this game, which largely has focused on female clothes; I haven't traditionally been that impressed with EA's offerings for male Sims--either they lack a certain masculinity or seem overly twee or simplistic. These are fashion-forward clothes for men that actually look like stuff a normal guy would wear. There are skinny jeans, as I guess we'll never escape those, but also normal-looking hoodies, T-shirts, trousers, and shorts. The only real off-note here is that some of the writing on the shirts is in Roman letters, not in Simlish, but I don't reckon most people will mind all that much and most of the letters are "stencils," which means they're painted atop the clothes and EA has thoughtfully given variants for these shirts without the stencils. The textures of the pants especially look really nice and realistic, but not garishly texture-mapped like in the Katy Perry Stuff Pack.

I was much more dubious about the women's clothes, but very quickly became a convert. They're really nice! The walkthroughs and box art don't do them justice at all. The shirts aren't dumpy, as I'd thought, or fussy; they're tailored and feminine, with neat little touches like hemstitching. The T-shirts have interesting designs on them, and the trousers are realistic and well-fitted. Yes, skinny jeans abound, but there's a cool pair of flares that I'll use often.

So overall I think these clothes would greatly appeal to anybody who wants to significantly add to their adult Sims' clothing choices, especially people like me who aren't generally impressed at all with how EA does men's clothes. I was impressed by the good execution, the stylish vision involved, and the sheer number of clothes offered in this pack.

Of the 10 or so objects, they're not bad. The end table and coffee tables are really cool-looking; the bed, with recoloring, looks interesting and stylish. I love the mirror--it hangs well just about anywhere as an accent. The lamps are all right but not as nice-looking ingame as I'd thought they'd be. There's a white twill upholstered easy chair that is very casual and suitable for most rooms. I see this SP's objects working beautifully with "Contemporary Comfort" and the rock-and-roll sets. If you like this sort of furniture and deco stuff, you'll like Diesel's offerings quite a bit as they are well-executed. If you're more traditional, you might not.

I rated this pack so highly because it does exactly what it advertises. It does not pretend to be for all age groups and it is straightforward regarding the low number of objects and lack of hairs/accessories. If you want those things more than clothes, you're probably better off leaving this SP on the shelf. If you just want clothes and you like this sort of style, it's a great SP, one of the stronger clothes-emphasized ones.

title: Absolutely one of the best games of its year.
text:
A RTS citybuilder with style, Anno 1404's expansion "Venice" hits the spot. It adds more missions and cool easter eggs to the already-fantabulous 1404 base game, along with new graphics and a retooled look. Combat makes more of an appearance here, but mostly it's an economy/balance game. You play a faction seeking dominance over all the rest. You create trade routes, scout new islands, and complete missions and quests to achieve your goals. As you gain population on each island, the citizens' needs expand--peasants will start wanting exotic spices, for example, but spices can only be gotten on the Middle Eastern-themed islands, so you end up building an intertwined trade network. When you get enough citizens on an island, you can start building huge projects like a humongous cathedral or Sultan's mosque, which convey distinct benefits to the islanders living nearby. And eventually you can purchase "seats" on each island's Council, which gives you influence over the governments there--and allows you to buy an opponents island out from under him.

Being able to create automated trade routes helps enormously with the micromanaging aspect of the game, allowing you to concentrate on the important stuff. The interface is blessedly simple and the game itself delightfully free from bugs and glitches. There are long-term missions, but the sandbox mode is the most fun, with each map having a distinct number in the database (and once you find a map you like, like 39950, you can enter it into the "generator" to use it again and again). Vast replay value ahoy!

One utterly charming thing about the game is that it gives you "awards" based on both serious and lighthearted things--anything from "you sank X number of enemy ships" to "you've hit pause X number of times." The announcer also thoughtfully warns you when you've been playing for 2, 4, and probably longer hours (I'm not admitting anything) so you can, as it suggests "go get a cup of coffee." If you happen to be playing on Valentine's Day, it'll thoughtfully give you a "rose" announcement and wish you all the best.

Last, I'm not sure if I mentioned this, but the graphics on "Venice" are sheer delight. The level of detail is astounding; it almost feels like overkill. Grass waves. Ships sway while docked in the harbor. Individual citizens visit theaters, swerve drunkenly arm-in-arm home from pubs, dance around maypoles, paint huge portraits, go shopping, and talk to their friends. You can zoom in quite a ways, rotate the screen, dip and swoop behind the dolphins swimming behind your ship, make this thing do whatever you want visually. The graphics alone would qualify this game as a contestant for Game of the Year.

As someone else said, thank goodness Germans are apparently way into these kinds of games, because it means awesome titles like Anno will get made. If you're American and haven't ever heard of this (I hadn't till I signed up for a European gaming service), definitely try it. You will not be disappointed. And if you're an American game designer, please play close attention: this is the right way to do a RTS.

title: Aims But Misses
text:
Physically, the mouse shape is a low, not filling a medium-sized hand, but has a nice ridge on the right side of the mouse, that almost lets the user grip it. The mouse weight is light enough for extended use. The mouse is covered with a thin coat of rubber-like material, but that material is somewhat slippy, because neither the mouse nor the coating has any texture. With the mouse shape, and coating, the mouse is not that grippy.

The buttons and scroll wheel are excellent, and well placed. The mouse wheel, unlike the rest of the mouse is very grippy, with a rubber ring around it. The extra buttons are reachable, but not in my way. I like that the extra buttons aren't large, flimsy, or heavy.

The lighting, though frustrating would be novel if it all of it could stored in the mouse. As the computer boots, the mouse shows a colored mess. The front light is a great idea. I suspect that the overall durability of the mouse has been compromised so that Corsair can have their logo light up. I worry, that the rubber material will wear off, leaving an ugly white mouse body behind. The mouse wheel lighting is a good feature, which makes it quick to find the mouse, if you take your hand from it.

The cord is braid-covered, and nice and long, but sadly, not user replaceable. Neither strain reliefs are pliable enough to function as strain reliefs. The USB plug body is excessively long, providing too long of a lever arm.

The software needs usability testing. You do things on one side of the screen, that cause buttons to appear on the other side of the screen. There are thing that are really going to need some experimentation to discover. The software itself takes up over 400mb.

It's disappointing that many settings are not saved in the mouse, leaving your computer to boot up with odd colors, and likely no stored keystrokes available.

The mouse software involving the DPI and colors is buggy.

My first day, I found a surface that made the mouse skip, which is a stark reminder that this is not a laser mouse. Standford University's excellent printed booklets made great ad-hock mousepads, but the Corsair Sabre, skips and chokes, mousing on a printed page. On a real cloth-covered mousepad, it seems to work well.

The price point for the mouse is excellent, but there's no reason why the Sabre's software and memory issues need to exist. Still, the mouse needs to be grippier, because at times the needs to lift the mouse.

title: This may be the single player Jedi game we have all been looking for!!!!
text:
The game is surprisingly good and while I had optimism as a fan of Respawns Titanfall series combined with the underrated great single player campaign they delivered in Titanfall 2, EA has unfortunately been EA while on a bad run lately. There have also been issues with both Battlefront games so while the gameplay looked interesting in footage that was shown I feared a bait and switch. Luckily this is not the case as you feel like a powerful Jedi who escaped Order 66 and without spoiling too much of the plot seek redemption from your own guilt. The graphics are beautiful (although some NPC characters clearly have less detail) and with this being the last big name multiplayer title release for the year it ends 2019 on a high note.
The game is so much fun because it truly has the best light saber feel I have felt in any Star Wars game so far. I do wish there were some more force powers but honestly not too many makes the most sense within the context of the story and they are used well. The combat is great too and feels very satisfying especially when you execute some instant kill animations. A possibly helpful recommendation that helped me is take out the ranged attackers first before focusing on others.
The story is pretty good so far and the characters like your mentor Cere Junda and new droid BD-1 are well done. Without spoiling things there are also some cameos of Star Wars characters we know and references to other legendary Star Wars events. It feels like Respawn did a great job of taking elements of other great video game series and incorporating them into the game with their own spin. There is definitely a Souls feel to the combat with an importance placed on timing and blocking. I also love the instant kill reward if you time things correctly with an enemy. In no way would I say this game is as difficult as a Souls game but it has a challenge that can ramp up considerably (however after each “death” the game does not get even more difficult). The enemies do all regenerate on a level if you decide to heal yourself though. There is of course a skill tree as well to develop Cal over time. There are also clear elements of Metroid Prime when you move around the map and an Uncharted/Tomb Raider style adventure feel as you traverse certain areas. You will also definitely revisit previously unreachable areas on planets but it’s fun to go back to areas in planets with more power/skill and the shortcuts you unlock allow for a different path. The game feels very rewarding when you play through and pretty smooth with limited pop ins.
I hope we see more games in this series and that this is a sign of where EA’s future single players games will go. A quality experience not bogged down with microtransactions. I love this game and recommend it highly for any Star Wars or Adventure game fans or for any people who want a more forgiving Souls experience. It is actually hard to put down and I look forward to playing through it again on the highest difficulty.

title: Strongest entry so far?
text:
While HeartGold and SoulSilver will hold a special place in my heart as my favorites, Black 2 (I refer only to Black 2 in this review, though most commentary is transferable to White 2 as well) is a strong entry in the Pokemon series without a doubt,and may objectively be the best so far.

Game Freak made a surprising move in announcing "Black and White 2", as no games had ever had direct sequels before - immediately visiting a new region ought to have killed the game while it was still an idea. It made it through somehow though, and I'm glad it did, because these games are packed so full of new content I have no doubt that I got my money's worth. From the new storyline to new areas to the medal system (a nod to Steam's "Achievements" and the like), there's no doubting that Game Freak took pains to make this a world worth revisiting.

All the old favorites are present (all... what, 649 of them) and some Pokemon come in new forms as well. The new starting area is especially appreciated, as starting off exactly the same way B/W did would have started things off on an old, expired note. Also updated is the necessity of HMs - once a painful bane of a gamer's existence, they've been almost entirely eliminated from the main story, instead serving as paths to extra areas. And my are there extras, though I'd prefer not to say much about them to keep the review relatively spoiler-free.

The game starts slow as usual, and the graphics have received little update, always a weak point of the series. Likewise, the plot is thin (though in recent games, has shown some improvement, especially in B/W and here). However, combat is as finely-tuned as ever, and if you live around many other Pokemon fans, there is no end in the ways to compete. It's always a little harder on those living in Poke-isolation, and while wifi takes some steps to relieve that, the "Pal Pad" is always a burden.
Still, these are minor issues in comparison to the big picture. Pokemon has always been strong, and Black 2 is another, if surprising, improvement to the franchise.

title: OLD COACH'S DREAM COME TRUE!
text:
This is my all-time favorite Madden game. I specifically purchased this year's version because I am a dinosaur and not terribly coordinated, making all those dazzling jukes and perfect timing pass routes extremely difficult. This was the last year that Madden was more of a coaching strategy game than a joy-stick game.
The only problem I had was it doesn't work on my computer because anything past Windows XP or 2000, doesn't recognize the program. This is where it pays to have friends. One of my friends has, what looks to me, a computer museum. Seriously, this guy has stuff going back to Commodores (not the group; the computer brand), and gave me a perfectly good older ASUS computer that runs on Windows XP. TOUCHDOWN!
One interesting aside about Madden 2003. Obviously, you can draft and coach your own team, but be aware that you get the playbook that came with whichever franchise you picked (Colts, Ravens, etc.), so if you pick a team that was primarily a West Coast offense, your playbook will be heavily skewed in that direction.
Here's the part I love the best. I love to coach the team because it's like a chess match. A lot of the other football games I have played make adjustments at half-time. Not Madden! If you play Pro level, the computer adjusts on the fly! Even though George W. couldn't say it, "Fool Me Once, Shame On You. Fool Me Twice, Shame On Me!". (No wonder we're still mired in Iraq almost 15 years later, with no end in sight.).
This is a very challenging game for folks who love to try to out-coach your opponent. Leave it to Amazon to locate something hard to find. THANX! Tim Drain.

title: Etrian Odyssey IV: Legends of the Titan
text:
I hadn't heard of this game, or seen any reviews, but when I saw it on the new releases, I decided to pick this up on a whim. Sometimes such impulse buying can get you burned, like the recent SimCity release. But this game is certainly not one of those.

It is a nice mix of classic dungeon crawling using some of the newest technologies. If you're not familiar with dungeon crawling, basically you start out at a base town with a few services (buy, sell, etc), and then venture into a dungeon, but there is more than one dungeon in this game.

Also similar to some of those old school crawlers, usually you can only save the game while in town. You can make restore saves, which get deleted as soon as you start playing again, and there are a few special save points in the dungeons. But if you die in this game, you won't be doing the typical save/load routine. And yes, you'll die. And probably often.

The game is a bit difficult. There are two settings, normal and easy, but I am playing it on normal. The overall story is just to go out and explore, but don't be reckless. Recklessness will ultimately harm you, as will complacency. There are even a few early encounters that (try to) teach you the detrimental effects of being complacent.

Different than many modern games, where the dungeons are side-notes and the maps are fully revealed, where you can beef up and go nuke anything that moves without worrying about dying. So don't get trapped into EZ mode thinking here.

There are a few other features in the game that make it unique:

Primarily is the mapping system. If you've played any of the classic dungeon crawl games that did not have mapping systems, you might remember the old pen-and-paper maps we'd draw as you explore the dungeons. While the game has an auto-mapper feature, it's by no means perfect. You'll use the 3DS stylus to draw walls, make iconic notes, paint water, and so on. The maps are saved even at the dreaded "game over", so that particular hard work is not lost. Get used to mapping, it's necessary, and actually quite fun and enjoyable. Get used to spinning around in a 360 degree circle, and checking to make sure there are no secrets.

Oh, how I wish we had this kind of mapping system back in the days of the Bard's Tale!

Somewhat related to the mapping system is the auto-play. You can place various movement icons on the map (left, right, up, down), and press "START", and the game will automatically move in those directions. Kinda like a macro, but not a fully automatic. You can map out a circular patrol pattern so that you can keep walking around the dungeons waiting for random encounters, without having to keep pressing buttons. I know some players will frown on such "auto levellers", but try it. It eases the grinding which seems to be inevitable in these kinda games.

Another nice feature is the content delivery system. The developer blog posts QR codes to unlock items, quests, and so on. So far, there are only two such postings, but I hope they continue doing so. You use an in-game feature to access the QR system.

Like a lot of newer 3DS games, they try to incorporate StreetPass, which is interesting, altho since I purchased my 3DS during the initial release in January 2011, I've only gotten a single Mii Plaza StreetPass tag. But I'll still hope to see if I get other tags. Apparently you can acquire new characters in this manner.

Finally of note is the music and the graphics, which are also just as good. The graphics are nicely drawn, also evoking nostalgia for hand-drawn graphics, instead of perfectly rendered 3D models. The package I picked up even had a CD of the OST; dunno if the version being sold on Amazon does as well, since it does not specifically note it.

All in all, if you like old school hack-n-slash dungeon crawling games, you'll probably like this game. If you've never played one before, why not give it a try?

title: Suprisingly Great Game, Better than Nocturne
text:
Before I played this game I played SMT: Nocturne. I was impressed with the game mechanics, as well as delighted with the difficulty of the game (unlike FF games, it was possible to be wiped out by even low level monsters if you weren't careful). So, when I saw another game sporting the SMT engine was coming to the PS2 I reserved it immediately.

Frankly I found this game to be better than SMT:N in most respects. True you don't get to create an "army" of monsters as in SMT:N (probably one of the better features of SMT:N), but you do have a greater control of the growth of your characters than you did in SMT:N (you no longer loose forever the skills that you replace).

So here is a breakdown of the game:

Plot: 4/5 Very good plot, somewhat confusing, but most of us who play Japanese games and read Mangas are used to being kept in the dark about what is really going on (as well as spending much of the earlier moments confused as hell... Big-O is a great example of this). Much like Xenosaga, there is a lot of information available that can be used to help figure things out, but you have to pay attention and be ready to think a little outside the box. The only thing I disliked was the use of the "silent protagonist". I hate this technique with a passion, where the main character is only given choices every once and a while, and in the meantime doesn't say a single word. Some of you may be familiar with this technique, as it's been used in a lot of games, such as Chrono trigger (and cross as well), SMT:N, the Breath of Fire games, and a couple of the Suikoden games (the first one for sure). The reason I dislike this technique? It causes the main character to be flat, shallow, and pretty much iconic. Basically, it prevents a lot of possible character development for who should be the focus of the plot. But with the Silent Protagonist character, you can only learn about the main character through others, and the others are of course allowed to reach a depth the main character cannot obtain. In SMT:DDS the main character "Serph" is the allowed only to reach a state that I would call "Robotic." There are a couple of moments where he is portrayed as having more depth, but those are fleeing and overall you are left with a character who seems to lack a personality. This aside, the other characters are developed fairly well, with enough left unknown to merit the sequel.

Graphics: 3/5 Good. This was made stright up using the SMT engine from nocturne. They even kept most of the demons from nocturne. The backgrounds and dungeons are somewhat drab, but that is done intentionally because of the setting in which the game takes place. The only negative side to the graphics is that sometimes the resolution is somewhat low, which can lead to problems with positioning.

Sound: 5/5 Excellent. This is one of the few successes in voice acting I've seen in a dubbed video game recently. While the voice acting isn't the best in the world, it at least portrays the characters well, and the lines aren't given with a constant tone of wooden indifference. There are a couple of voices that don't quite hit the mark, but the core cast is very well done. The music is excellent, many of the tunes fit the atmosphere, and the introduction reel by Etero Anime fits the intro scene.

Control: 5/5 Great. The controls are almost exactly as they were in SMT:N. The battle system uses the same attack number determination as well. Most controls are straight forward, although the battle system is more complex for those used to FF turn based style combat. But if you pay attention and read up on the combat, it becomes second nature after a while.

Novelty: 2/5 Below average. This is the one low point of the game. It is unfortunate that they chose to keep so many of the monsters from SMT:N. It made the game feel more like a mod than an actual self enclosed game. By keeping so much of the SMT:N system they pretty much lost all ability to consider the game a novel creation. Although DDS is a great game, if you've played nocturne, you'll find yourself saying "hey wait a minute I've seen this before" quite a bit. The plot is quite original, as is many of the items and some new skills. But for the most part, it feels like you are playing a game with 40% new material and 60% recycled material.

Overall: 5/5 It's a great game despite a few flaws. If you liked SMT:N then you'll love this game. If you hated SMT:N or found it frustratingly difficult, then you'll find this game much the same.

title: A Good Last Expansion Pack for the Series.
text:
Though it's a little uneven, this last expansion pack (EP) for the Sims 3 has undeniable charms for someone interested in futuristic, science-fiction Simming.

This EP adds a variety of SF-themed special objects, clothes, and hairs to the game. From "Back to the Future" hoverboards (think "flying skateboards") to jetpacks like Calvin's dad wore in the fantasy segments of the old comic strip, to nanotech research and robot building centers, to weird portals, to the way even the potted plants look like they came straight out of a "Star Trek" reboot movie, there's a lot here to look at and enjoy. It's not going to add a lot to the regular game without completely wrecking its ambience, though, and Simmers who prefer a more medieval, goth, realistic, urban/gritty, or fantasy feel to their game aren't going to appreciate a lot from this EP. The decor and new wall/floor textures are to say the least utilitarian, and while it's all utterly thematic to a science fiction experience, it's not very useful elsewhere--except for transparent glass panel flooring tiles that I love in club venues and grass-textured "carpets" that can be used indoors in greenhouses (thus eliminating unwanted "unfinished room" moodlets)--YAY! Those are extremely welcome.

A new "life state" is introduced here: PlumBots, which are playable robots that can be built ingame from components and whose personalities are determined by chips installed into them. There's a lot of variety to these bots; they can be very simple and sticklike to very complicated and stolid, and of course can be just about any color you want. With the appropriate chipset, they can do just about anything that a regular Sim can do--but their limitations can make them quite a lot of fun all on their own.

And of course there are new collectibles added by the EP. Nanites, new insects, special digsites and the like pepper the landscape. A new style of refrigerator/sink can synthesize the EP's new recipes quite easily as well. New skills include playing a SF-style harp, flying with the jetpack, and eating bugs.

Once the EP's special world (Oasis Landing) is visited, one can easily see the influence of pop SF like "The Hunger Games" in the clothes and hairs, but as with most of the series, sly references are inserted regarding everything from "Futurama" and "Castle" to "Game of Thrones." There's even an old hermit in robes living in a little cabin by himself at the edge of a bleak desert with a name suggesting a certain fellow from an iconic SF movie from years ago. The city itself looks completely inorganic and planned, with flat terrain, carefully laid out roads, and swathes of solar cells in fields. But stray from the city and you'll find a very different picture; the have-nots live in little mining neighborhoods or out in what looks for all the world like the Dune Sea, where treasures await the ambitious--and where a downed spacecraft bears secrets of its own. Even more entertainingly, anything significant your Sims do in the "real" world can influence how their descendants do--and even how that future world looks. And of course your Sims can visit those descendants and interact with them all.

I will say that I pretty much hate almost every single bit of clothing and hair in this EP. The rabbitholes are GORGEOUS and I love the venues EA has made, and their premade Sims/households are as usual outstanding and cheeky. But the clothing and hairs are just ugly to me. Your mileage may vary. It all looks like it was designed by Lady Gaga after watching "The Hunger Games" on auto-repeat for a few weeks.

All in all, if you like science-fiction Simming, you'll like this EP. If you don't like that stuff, chances are you won't really enjoy this EP as much. I held off on getting it for a long time and picked it up only once it went on serious sale, and I'm generally happy with what it's brought my game for the price I paid. I haven't used much of it in my normal gaming though. This is a very specific EP aimed at a very specific audience and it's not going to appeal to absolutely everybody, but if you're one of those people, then you can purchase it in confidence.

title: Burned
text:
The short version: don't buy this game.

Any innovative features are buried under the fundamental flaws that exist in the game. I only wish I waited a week after release, but now I'm out $80 with nothing but a not-so-warm and happy feeling that I've spent my money on a product which implies my endorsement this type of system, and by purchasing the game, I've contributed to the mess that is the video games industry by spending my money to support online-only DRM.

Out of the almost 2,000 reviews here, various gaming blogs and other news sites, if you're not already aware, this game has the 100% necessary requirement of online play. If your internet is down, no game for you.

Basically, you're leasing this game, and only under the good graces of EA. If they decided to shut the game down, you can't play. No online, no play. Servers overloaded, no play. This is NOT an MMO, where you are logging in to a server to play a game, this is DRM (digital rights management) which is the authentication method used to verify the license of the game.

Oh sure, they'll eventually fix it, and they've already promised us a free game, currently unidentified, from the EA catalog, but don't be surprised if it's some kind of bargain-barrel game. But what they HAVEN'T promised is a method to fix the online-only DRM, so their promise of a free game is just to dangle a carrot in front of us in the hopes that we'll forget how thoroughly they're burning us.

The DRM method used is the new trend in video games, and the only way to express your dissatisfaction is to NOT buy the game. Compare this to video games ~10 years ago, where you got a CD, and you can install the game at any time. Nope, even if you got the physical media for this game, you might not be able to play this next year, or whatever. I can pull out my old Doom or Quake games, each easily over 10 years old, and still play them today.

Social features of this game aside, this is NOT an MMO (I know I'm repeating myself). 100% online is not a requirement for a game like this.

Save your money, send a message, don't buy it.

title: Lack of info for PS3 controllers, and terrible design.
text:
I have two complaints.

Complaint #1
-----------------
They really leave you in the wind with this product. I figured it out, but I'm wondering about people who are not as resourceful. The description implies you just plug it into the Switch, and you start pairing. That is not the case, at least it's not the case for PS3 controllers. There are no instructions, so naturally, I went to 8bitdo's website. On their site, there is something called the PS3 PAIRING TOOL. Sounds like what I need, so I downloaded it. In the downloaded folder is a README file. How often do people read the README files? Luckily I did! It says that before I can launch the software, I need to install a program called the SixaxisPairToolSetup-0.3.0.exe, or I can "Temporarily disable driver signature enforcement." For this 2nd option, there is a bunch of screenshots showing you how to do it in windows. I tried the 1st option first, and after installing the sixaxispairtool, it told me to restart. After restarting, normally a software will launch itself to help you along where you left off, but not this one. Once you restart, it was gone. LOL! So I thought maybe the magic has been done, so I proceeded to launch the PS3 pairing tool, but it didn't work. It would not recognize my ps3 controller. So I decided to try the second option, temporarily disable driver signature enforcement. For this option, I recommend you guys put all the instructional screenshots in your dropbox, then you can follow along reading the instructions from your phone. Because doing these steps will put you in a RECOVERY mode, so you can't view those screenshots anymore. They didn't make this accessory for everybody. They made it for techies and tinkerers who will go out of their way to make it work.

Complaint #2
----------------
8bitdo isn't too good at adapter designs. Take their Gbros adapter for example. It doesn't fit wavebird receivers, not because it isn't compatible, but because of the design. So Retro Fighters basically just built a new shell for that receiver and fixed the issue. So it isn't too surprising to me that this wireless receiver is a bad design too. title: You�ll know when you need it.
text:
Don't buy this memory card until you need it. Mine works well, but it only has one use: it transfers files from X-box to X-box.
The X-box has a huge hard drive, and since the hard drive is what you use to save your games, you can play for years without a memory card.
After fully testing the memory card, here are the restrictions:
-You can't directly transfer files from X-box to X-box, even with the system link cable, so the only way to transfer files is with the memory card.
-You can't transfer music files on the memory card. It would hold about two files, but the X-box won't let you. You can only transfer game saves.
-You can only transfer character profiles, so you can't transfer the progress on a game like Dead or Alive that doesn't have character profiles.
-You have to transfer character profiles one at a time.
Probably the best use for this memory card is if your friend has an X-box, and has unlocked a bunch of special features on a game, you can save the profile off your friend's X-box to your memory card and then transfer it to your X-box.

Tons to do...all original main story which I thoroughly enjoyed and was surprised by the ending, battle coliseum, and Transtown....lots of mini-games, fishing, bug catching, exploring, collecting. Plenty of quests are on the game without any dlc....and are replayable. The game does mark ones that have been completed. This version offers two ----yes two save slots!

Custom Words are collected phrases that are equipped and changeable that do effect abilities in battle. Example--Program Chopper with the custom words and he yells, "I'm a doctor!" while healing you in battle, the phrase itself also ups his healing power. This can add hours of depth alone and keeps you fom hearing the same phrases all the time because it also changes the phrases your character yells in battles. All spoken dialogue is in Japanese....and there is a TON of voice work even in battles
but don't worry....you get subtitles that don't intrude. Run around---town and npc speak...tap your R button when it flashes on the screen and you
respond appropriately...little things like that make for a very enjoyable time. Battles also have timed actions as well as button combos. You'll love some of the moves you pull off! Easy, medium and hard are difficulty choices you can change during the game as well.

I have nothing negative at all to say about this gorgeous, colorful, exciting game and am really impressed with it. I've only been playing video games since 1977...lol...

title: 2 for 2, failed buttons. Just get a Deathadder
text:
I wanted to like this mouse. I like the position of the buttons (particularly the toggle DPI that lets you have a "snipe" button - more mice need that) and the general shape of the mouse, but it's just got so many problems, including abysmal build quality (which is shocking for logitech)

For starters, it's weirdly draggy and a bit heavy, even wired and with zero weights in it. I can't see anyone wanting to add more of the included weights - the point of this kind of mouse is to start LIGHT and let you tune it, not start heavy and let you make it worse. Genuinely heavier than my full size WIRELESS teknet mouse that I use for my media PC.

The feet lasted okay, they're starting to feel worn after a year of use on an aluminum banshee pad mousepad (I usually got about 2-3 years out of a set of feet on a Razer Deathadder) And they're very sensitive to picking up schmutz. Replacement feet are not readily found, you're gonna be using teflon tape. The combination of really meh feet and really heavy/draggy weight makes the mouse wildly imprecise after only a couple months. Even with teflon tape over the feet, I still can't make a "clean" drag across my mousepad with a smooth cursor movement. Not even sure it would when it was new. The aforementioned teknet mouse still absolutely glides after years. I think it's just because the 502 has SIX absolutely gigantic pads, and other mice I use tend to have 3 or 4 much smaller feet at most, which keeps the inherent friction lower.

Cord is okay if used with a mouse bungie.

The scroll wheel is abysmal. It has a side/side rock, which is already not good for a proper gaming mouse (they all have a habit of mis-registering mouse 3 clicks) but this is easily the worst I've ever experienced. I am used to the design, but this one is so bad and vague that I had to straight up disable the rocker, so now I only get about 15% of my middle clicks mis-sensed. The ability to unlock a scroll wheel is nice when I have to turbo scroll through a 300 page document, but again, in GAMING practice, is just one more way the scroll wheel feels incredibly vague and inaccurate.

mouse 4 is just set too far back. You have to press it with the knuckle of your thumb, which requires an incredibly awkward "palm pinch". If you use all the mouse buttons in a game, you're going to hate this thing so much.

And the thing is INCREDIBLY fragile. My first one's left click broke just sliding off my chair onto carpet, the whole mouse button itself sheared off. The second one's L2 switch itself is now failing, as it registers right click but doesn't register HOLDING it. After only a year, this is appalling. If you play MMO's, this makes steering an absolute nightmare. If you play FPS games, right click iron sight/scope becomes agony.

And there's something about this mouse that gives me really sweaty palms, which is weird because I have a kind of hybrid palm/fingertip grip that keeps my palm usually hovering just above the mouse

My deathadder was only replaced by this mouse because I suspected the skin flakes embedded in the chassis had evolved a new form of life. This one is getting hucked in the garbage because it fell to pieces in a little over a year and a half. I am staying away from Logitech for a few years after two absolutely atrocious peripherals and going back to the good old iron duke of a Razer Deathadder.

title: Great Rendition of a Classic Game ...
text:
I bought this as a sneaky attempt to get my wife into playing video games. It didn't hurt that we both enjoy competing against each other every night at 7:30 while watching the actual show. Not knowing how well this game was going to work on the Wii, I pulled out all stops and ordered the WiiSpeak as well (which seemed to be the only logical way to create a more authentic Jeopardy! experience). While I think the game is definitely fun and a worthy purchase, there are a few frustrations that shouldn't come as surprising.

First, the positives:
- the game offers a realistic Jeopardy! experience visually ... everything on the show is represented in this game (from the occasional quirky categories to the sage-like mannerisms of the Alex Trebek Mii character.

- you can customize your Mii with items you earn by winning and with the WiiSpeak, you can even record "happy" and "sad" exclamations when you answer a question right or wrong (however the repetitive nature of the exclamation can be irrititating).

- the categories are varied and deep. Like the real Jeopoardy!, you can end up with a whole board of categories you have no clue about ... chalk one up for the educational quality of video games.

- the game allows you to modify the difficulty level, response method and time allowed to respond.

- The mini-games between Jeopardy! rounds are fun and allow you to win items to customize the game.

- The optional WiiSpeak is not a requirement to play this game.

Now, the drawbacks (which are mostly associated with the Wii itself):
- Although the WiiSpeak is optional, it is preferable for realism. The problem I experienced is that it only seems to work if: the settings on the WiiSpeak are perfect, you speak in a clear, concise and loud manner and there is not a single sound being made outside you answering the question. In other words, if you have a dog, kids or the dishwasher going or if everyone is laughing and enjoying themselves ... forget it. The sensitivity adjustments for the WiiSpeak are not always helpful either.

- Being able to type responses requires a keyboard in my opinion and using a Wii controller to spell words was frustrating for me personally (thankfully spelling the first few letters will generate a list of answers to choose from as a shortcut). The game does offer a multiple choice option for answers that eliminates the need to spell the answer, but I didn't like seeing all the answers. I don't fault the game for this as it generously gives the player three answering methods to choose from before the game begins.

- I am not aware of the opportunity to expand the database of answers in the future.

Overall, I think this is a great rendition of the real thing ... fun and challenging. I'm not a fan of spelling with a controller, but the more I play, the more I see improvement in my "console controller dexterity". I think most Jeopardy! fans would enjoy this game.

title: It's okay if you buy it cheap.
text:
This game is okay, if you buy it cheap. It's extremely linear, with not much of a story. It has some interesting things going for it, and a lot of bad. The game appears to be an open world, but it's not. It appears to be big, but there is really not a lot of things going on it. If your expecting Skyrim, run fast and far away.

The game has a ton of bugs in it. My favorite is water skiing off a mountain into water, and then drowning. I must have performed that move 20 or 30 times before I stopped going near ledges. Do not go near a ledge, or prepare to water ski off a ledge I drowned in a foot of water once, that was special. You think the game developers could have taught the bastard to swim! Another fantastic bug is when you got up close and personal fighting something, and your character goes into an epileptic fit. Your weapon gets put away, comes out put away, etc. The only way to fix this was to move away, then re-attack. The game had a lot of potential, but it's almost like the game company ran out of money and did as little as possible to finish it. Weapons and items were okay, nothing exciting. Anything worth buying cost way more money than you had. Here are a few Pros and Cons, which hopefully will help you make up your own minds on whether to purchase the game.

Pros:
1) Like a normal RPG, you can level up various skills throughout the game.
2) You can play as a fighting, magic using, or mixed skills character.
3)The world is gorgeous in places, including how they rendered the ocean.
4) Using magic is fun and looks cool.
5) Shooting enemies with a range weapons looks cool.
6) The way some of the enemies blend in with their surrounding is nice. Especially the Panthers. Though that's in the DLC.

Cons:
1) The area seem large, but there isn't really a lot going on in them.
2) There's not a ton of different enemies to fight.
3) I bought 100 arrows, that's it. Money was basically worthless.
4) Items being sold are so overpriced that you can only buy a couple of them throughout the game.
5) The game runs clunky, and things seem to pixelate a lot.
6) The quests are all fetch this and that. Boring and repetitious.
7) There is only a few people to talk to in each inhabited area.

So in my opinion if you can get this game cheap, and need and need a game to play, buy it. Just don't expect to much from it.

title: Apart From the L2/R2 Snag, Totally Fine
text:
This controller arrived during the last week of July, 2017.

Have been using it to play Final Fantasy XIV on my PC (Windows 10) for several hours per day since then. (Ok, 12-18 hours per day; I keep it on while writing, typing, transcribing, programming, etc.) It's not STRAIGHT usage, but I'd consider it heavy usage, nonetheless.

Anyway, it's now a few minutes into 29 October, 2017, and the poor controller began to show its age a few days ago, hence my frantic trip over here; you know the symptoms: your character can't move in a straight line, or else keeps running in circles, etc.
In my case, it's also that the system doesn't recognise a hard right turn on the right analogue stick (though I can still press it and get into first-person mode).

Am beyond tempted to open this thing up and see if some dog hairs or whatnot got in there (like the old skool mouses (mice?) that you'd have to clean out every few days, or if the issue is related to springs or gaskets or what.
Truth is, though, that I'm not confident in my ability to pry it open without completely destroying the plastic housing, so let's wait till the replacement arrives, eh?

NOTE: The button-pressing on this thing was never the most... reliable? Like sometimes it would take a shallow half-press to register, other times, it took a major SMASH until the press "counted." It was like this from the beginning, but only got worse as time went on. Again, not sure if it's an issue or materials or dog hair.

I'm grateful for the few months this controller worked "well" (or "well-enough"), and would buy again.

One thing, however--and I don't know if it's related to the game itself, or all USB-for-PC controllers, or THIS controller or what--but the BOTTOM trigger buttons/"bumpers" (L2 and R2 or LT and RT) have NEVER been recognised by my system (again, Windows 10, and NOT Steam version of FF14).
Like, since Day One. I've calibrated and mapped and tweaked like it's going out of style but alas, it was for naught. For the record, I also have a wireless controller for my Mac (SteelSeries, purchased from Big A--well, the other Big A that isn't this one), and IT refused to recognise the D-PAD, of all things. (Yes, lots of frustrations around here, lol.)

Anyway, my experience with this product is limited to the one I got, but I WOULD buy again, and would also recommend to someone looking for a solution to a tech situation similar to mine--as long as s/he knew that this thing would likely have to be replaced "at some point in the near future," which applies to everything under the sun these days (even pricier items).

Happy gaming to all,
SB

title: Great Workout and Dance Moves.
text:
I only bought this tonight, but I spent a good amount of time trying it out since I got home.

I'm not familiar with the Kinect (also got it tonight), so this is my first time using the controls. I found the menu on this game extremely easy to use. You hold your hand around waist level and swipe your hand to select an option. I had to do it a few times on occasion, when I didn't swipe far enough, but overall, it wasn't a problem at all.

The game comes with only the first three or four songs unlocked, and you can unlock the rest. I don't like when games do this, but I had so much fun with this one that I don't care much. You can choose easy, medium or hard levels. You can select "Break It Down", which takes you through each step of the routine, and then has you do the moves in order, in chunks - 6 or 7 moves at a time. This makes it easy to remember what you're doing when you finish "Breaking It Down" and move into the performance mode. You see little "flashcards" on the side of the screen to let you know what move you should be doing, and what moves are coming up. I played the songs on Hard mode, and I almost aced them. I'm a good dancer, but I'm also out of shape and in the process of losing a lot of weight. I was surprised at how well I did - but, lest you think that this game is too easy - it's definitely not. I assume (especially after reading other reviews) that the moves will get much harder.

Best part is that when I was done, I was sweaty and breathing hard. I panicked at first, after seeing the moves, that they were too easy. But, when they're put together, they pack a punch.

The Kinect did a good job of recognizing all of my movements. When you do a movement wrong, even if you're just holding your arm too high, the area that you're not moving correctly lights up red on the on-screen dancer. The game does want you to be pretty precise, but it doesn't freak out on you if you're not perfect.

And, I'm not gonna lie. I like the dancers telling me how awesome I am. Sometimes you need to hear that :)

The absolute best part, though, is the fact that each song (at least the ones I've played) have a "Freestyle" section - a short break where you can dance however you like. After you're done, you can choose "Pictures" from the menu and it would show you a sped up and extremely hilarious video of you dancing freestyle. I wasn't expecting this, and my boyfriend and I had a laughing fit over it.

I haven't played the Battle mode yet, and I have a lot more exploring to do - but, I highly recommend this game. It's a great workout and the moves aren't stale and stupid. I could actually see learning some dance moves from this to incorporate into a night of real life dancing.

There is also a "Workout" mode that I haven't explored yet, that monitors your caloric burn.

So many of the new Kinect games seem to be duds. This is not one of them.

I highly recommend this game for just plain fun or for working out!

Hindsight tells me I should have waited for at least some critical reviews for a game whose price tag is as high as Nintendo's own AAA properties (which are usually worth their price, but that's another topic)

I have probably about 10 hours into the game, and my dragon is at the second stage; not sure how much more it'll grow, but I do not think I will find out. Loading times alone are not worth it, every zone-in is met with a loading screen. Sometimes you'll even get loading screens without zoning. The loading screens last long enough to interrupt any sense of engagement.

There are other issues, such the shampoo-rinse-repeat cycle you're involved with. Wake up, go downstairs and you'll probably be greeted with a cut scene that expands the current chapter. Once that is done, go outside and harvest ingredients until time runs outs, and it'll run out pretty fast because the clock is a tad bit faster than my comfort level.

The artwork is definitely beautiful, and I seem to recall seeing somewhere that the creator likens the game to a storybook unfolding, but like a storybook that is linear, that style doesn't quite fit this game model.

title: I've been looking for an affordable headset with surround.  This fit my needs.
text:
[[VIDEOID:bcce61b61b8337c3b68e072c0d20d249]] I had a USB gaming headset that worked fairly well. It had large speakers that gave the sound a "roomy" feeling, especially when paired with the driver software that it came with, but the wire was driving me crazy. I couldn't step away from my desk without removing a few things or I'd end up pulling away my computer with me.

So, I was in the market for a nice pair of wireless gaming headsets. I've come across many in the 30-dollar range but none of the descriptions for those touted surround sound. Eventually, I had to look in the 60 - 90 range.

This pair of OCG Gaming Headsets 2.4GHz Bluetooth Wireless Gaming Headphones were just what I needed. I wanted bluetooth capabilities because I wanted to have it as an option in case I wanted to pair it to two computers (one via dongle and one via bluetooth). I also wanted the option of using it with other gaming systems such as an XBox or Playstation. The usb dongle gives that versatility.

I really don't care much for RGB as they just make my computers distracting and I'm not a game streamer or youtuber (not yet, anyway, ha ha), but if you do like them, this headset has them...

So, what do I think? I'd been playing Uncharted 4 on my PC with my old pair of headphones and it sounded great. The surround didn't really seem like it worked very well. After I received the OCG, I plugged in the USB dongle and booted up the game. The game automatically detected the headset and showed that it was using virtual surround. Immediately, I found that I was hearing sounds that I hadn't heard before!

As the character walked around, I heard the jangling sounds of the equipment he had at his belt, I heard the companion character talking behind me and as I turned, her voice moved around my head. I was super impressed!

I then disconnected the dongle and tried the headset in bluetooth mode. The sound was a little muffled and there was almost no surround effect, even though the game still said that it was doing virtual surround.

So I'm definitely using the dongle for all my gaming. I love this thing!

Easily in my Top 10 games of all time - and I started playing games in the 1980's with Super Mario.

The open world feels big and open without feeling overwhelming, there are some areas that are innately more dangerous than others, usually because of the density of zombies in that particular area. The graphics are good and the developers are staying on top of updates - the released a fix for the patch that stopped the modders from legitimately modifying the game. Good job devs.

Gameplay is fun and enjoyable, I've finished the game and started playing it again. The story is engaging enough to keep playing, so I'm not knocking it. The melee combat is the best I've seen yet, although I'm not overly familiar with melee in games like Skyrim and Assassin's Creed. The parkour aspect of the game is enjoyable as well, it doesn't feel forced but it feels compelling, which is exactly how a feature should be implemented. The disturbing thought of running through the streets decapitating zombies is so weirdly cathartic, but it IS a release and is enjoyable. I haven't hooked my Xbox One controller up to the PC to play it that way, but if it's half as good as the PC controls then it'll be fine.

Overall, I would definitely recommend this game if you're looking for a fun hack and slash game with some deeper elements like decision making (do I go the long route or the densely populated route?) and some hopping from girder to girder. On a scale from Conan O'Brien to those-chainsaw-guns-from-Gears-of-War, I give this game 19 [Bolter's Flesh].

title: Great entry level mechanical board.
text:
Coming from a penny pincher background with limited keyboard experience, this board is great! In the past, I always opted for the cheaper, entry level keyboards. Never again!
I don't think I've used a keyboard with such a great tactile feel and satisfying audible feedback since my original IBM AT keyboard. The amount of force required to type is perfectly balanced, for me. I can rest my hands on the keys without accidental strokes. Previous membrane keyboards felt like they required more force to register strokes, so typing on the G610 feels effortless.
The backlighting makes it easier to use in low light setting. Although the board has a button that allows you to change brightness of the backlighting, the default setting is to have the keys light up in a 'wave'. Since the human eye is attracted to motion, I find it very distracting to have a wave of light travel across my keyboard. I wish the default setting was to have a constant backlighting, so this is where my rating falls to 4 stars. I'd prefer to not install more software on my PC, but I was forced to install Logitech's software to control the backlighting.
Another minor complaint is the placement of the caps lock/scroll lock/num lock indicator lights. To make room for media control buttons, the indicator lights were moved to the top middle of the board, where it is not so intuitive to figure out which light is which. There are labels etched under each light, but they are unreadable, even in decent lighting levels.
Overall, I would highly recommend this board to anyone.

text:
I have bought many gaming headphones over the years. These are not USB headphones, which is what has become very popular over the past decade.

I like to use a good sound card as I have ears that work and I can tell the difference. A USB headset totally ignores the sound card as it uses the USB, which does not go through it, making the sound card irrelevant. This headset connects to the sound card, utilizing its full potential. The difference in sound is very distinct. This headset is so good that I bought two of them, one for each of my computers.

If you do not hear well and/or you are not good with differentiating sounds, use a cheap USB headset.

title: Great product - tape hinge method didn't work for me
text:
If you are unsure of which protector to choose for your Switch, I'd say you can't go wrong with Orzly. They make some of the thinnest protectors, and they're scratch proof. They are also cut more precisely to match the Switch screen than protectors from other makers. Some makers don't bother to cut out a shape for the light sensor, etc. Great product.

Onto application:

I'm a perfectionist with this kind of thing. It's definitely good that they include 2 pieces per kit because I screwed it up the first time & couldn't use the first piece. For the first attempt I tried the tape hinge method seen in various places on YouTube. That didn't work so well for me. I ended up having to reposition it, so I peeled it off and moved it a little, only to find a piece of dust trapped under it. I then tore it off and trashed it since cleaning both the screen and inside of the 1st protector seemed nearly impossible. I don't think you're actually supposed to use an alcohol wipe on the inside of a protector, and in any case I only had 1 more wipe. I moved on to the next attempt and simply eyeballed it as I set it down. I found that when I set it down the entire underside was still not adhered (i.e. it was all one big air bubble), so I could still shift it around a little to be perfect. I did this and then pressed down in the center to start the adhesive / bubble removal process. In the end I'm satisfied but this could've easily been a 1-star product if they hadn't included two protectors, or even if I couldn't do it in two tries. I imagine they (& other manufacturers) include two protectors based on the average number of attempts it takes or such.

title: A backward step from Forza 6
text:
While there were the expected improvements in graphics and new locations and features, the overall gameplay has suffered in a few key areas. My criticism comes from being a fan of this series since Forza 3.

Here are the problem areas that really represent an overall decline from Forza 6:
1. No Toyota. Obviously this is a probably some legal snafu that relates to licensing and competition with another video game title, but this has never been an issue in the past and Turn 10 hasn’t been really forthcoming with information.
2. For some reason, they’ve put this huge emphasis on the physical drivatar. Like, driver gear is now a huge facet of the prize game. Every non-race menu features your driver standing around shaking his limbs. It’s so awkward and pointless.
3. The game wants to auto-homologate your cars for you. I preferred the past versions where you knew what your race series required and modded your own car accordingly, with the auto-homologate being an option. You can still do your own modding, but the menu interface is much less intuitive for this.
4. Game AI is as bad as ever. On normal difficulty, you have to go from 11th place to 1st (realistically) in 3 laps which isn’t hard, but it really forces you to play bumper cars most of the time to accomplish that. An option to run a qualifying lap would really improve this issue.

Overall it’s still fun, but they’ve emphasized all the wrong features as part of the evolution. Hopefully updates in the near future will address these issues, but as of now, I’d recommend 6 over 7.
