title: Despite the price, it's a convenient tool to have
text:
After buying this through one of Amazon's partner sellers three years ago, I noticed no one has bothered to review this thing. I think it's about time someone stepped up, so I'm here to describe my experience with the XCM K.O. device. In the three years I've owned this, the XCM K.O. Gear has helped me earn a platinum trophy on the PS3 for the following fighting games: Blazblue (CT, CS & CS Extended), Soul Calibur V, Mortal Kombat vs DC Universe, Mortal Kombat and Marvel vs Capcom 3. Let's start with the basics.

**The Good**

-5 programmable memory buttons that can hold 20 button inputs in each memory slot: You can program any set of button combinations into this thing. It's perfect for complicated combos. Let's look at a small combination of buttons. Ibuki in Super Street Fighter IV has a great Ultra attack which requires you to do a half quarter circle twice + 3 of the punch buttons. When things get heated in a fight and I need to unleash this move, I have a hard time doing it because I suck at doing this properly on the d-pad. This is why the KO Gear is handy. I can program the Ultra attack before hand, so when I need to use it, I can just press the memory button and it will unleash it on the fly! You can even chain other combos together, which leads into the next topic.

-The difficulty in combo challenges diminish: Before I bought this, I hadn't completed a single combo challenge in MK vs DC Universe. But guess what? It only took me less than two weeks to do them all using this device. This is because you can link combos together using the KO Gear device. Let's say a combo requires you to do a multitude of inputs. If your button to eye coordination is bad and your memory sucks, you're in luck. You can program half of a combo string in one memory slot and the second half in another memory slot. Time it right and you can literally unleash a full combo string with just the press of two buttons. The KO Gear also remembers the timing of each button, so if a combo requires a late button input, the device will remember. Though sometimes the device may not register the combo correctly and it takes a bit of trial and error to get it right.

-It's an awesome learning tool: From what I noticed, people seem to define this device as a cheating tool. When I bought it, I even considered it as such. However, this device has taught me how to examine fighting games in advanced ways. Without this, I never would have paid attention to hit boxes, nor would have known how to cancel dash to continue combos. I wouldn't have known how to time my attacks on falling opponents to make sure they don't wake up in time to counter. Overall, I never would have learned that doing these combos isn't a natural born skill nor impossible, as it just takes time and practice. After entering so many combos, I began to learn and understand the timing of attacks. The repetition of button inputs, as well as trial and error, caused me to sometimes stop using the device and rely on my skill instead. This device has really helped me get better at my own pace and taught me methods that I thought were only reserved for fighting game pros.

-Good for non-combos and non-fighting games as well: Since this has a programmable turbo inputs, you can be creative in how this device can help you. For instance, in Soul Calibur V, there's a trophy called "Wind of Battle" which requires you to move over 87,600m throughout the game. You can set this device to do it for you by programming your movement and placing either a rubber band, book or tape over the memory button to keep it held down. You can use this to even get other trophies and achievements in non-fighting games. LittleBigPlanet 2 for example has a trophy for spending 24 hours in create mode and not be idle. With the KO Gear, you can set it to open and close the menu in the hub over and over. Just walk away from the PS3 and come back 24 hours later to see your trophy popped.

-The front light: It helps you see, especially if you're doing this in a darkly lit room.

**The Bad**

-The price is not ideal for this kind of technology: The price is a bit absurd. When people ask me if I think it's worth buying, I always say "it depends." If you have $80 to waste and have a bunch of fighting games in your catalog that you've put on the back burner because you have a hard time doing combo challenges in, then by all means go for it. If your the type of person that has just SFIV and KoF XIII on your shelf and think this may help you get a few trophies/achievements, seek out to buy a cheaper turbo controller instead. If your fighting gaming library is limited, you'd get a better value out of a controller than a macro device any day.

-Not ideal for charge characters: SFIV, SSFIV & KOF XIII have a lot of charge characters and this device doesn't work well with charge inputs. It takes too much trial and error to get it to work. For instance, Balrog in SFIV charge attacks work only in the beginning phase of a combo string. So I could only program the 1st half and do the rest of the string using my own skill.

-The cord is too short: I'm amazed the cord hasn't been ripped out of the device. You don't know how many times I've tripped over this thing. You have to be in a very close proximity due to its length.

-Sometimes it syncs the controller incorrectly: It's best to plug in the device before starting a game. When plugging a dual shock controller into it, the device will set the controller as player 2 or 3 and needs to be reassigned. It's not a big deal and only takes a few seconds to correct on the PS3 but it is annoying sometimes.

**Overall**

It's a great little tool to help you learn the basics and advance methods of every fighting game out there based on the repetition of button inputs you'll have to do. After a while, chaining combos will begin to feel natural and you won't need to use this anymore. It's great for a fighting game enthusiast that has a bad memory or just needs a little help to get past certain elements of gameplay they find to be a challenge. If you just have a single fighting game like Street Fighter IV, I honestly recommend a turbo controller or a fight stick over this. The price is what kills the value of the K.O. Gear. There are much better options out there.

EDIT: I also wanted to confirm that this doesn't work for the PS4. I think this might be because the PS4 controller uses digital input instead of analog. Try researching the Hori Pad FPS Plus controller, which has a turbo button, or look into the USB devices CronusMax or Titan One if you want something for PS4.

title: A review from an actual Fallout fangirl
text:
No reason to hate this game, not sure how people could buy this game without knowing it was online only. There was enough press for months and a huge launch at a gaming convention saying just that, "ONLINE GAMEPLAY ONLY." That's a not a reason to give it a one star review. That said, the game is freaking fantastic. One of my favorite things to do is wander the wasteland, build camps, and scrap, scrap, scrap.

Everything you love about the previous Fallout's is here. You start as level 1, you gather supplies, you learn how to make/modify armor, guns, ammo, water, food, etc. You will fight ghouls, mutants, scorchers, rad scorpions, radiated animals, and the like. Sure, there's no NPC's, but you will spend your time trying to figure out what happened to them through holo tapes. There are mini missions that help you rank up and earn perk points as well as stimpaks and water. Similar to Red Dead 2, you need to make food and purify water to stay alive, this is a pretty easy task.

In just a few hours of gameplay I ranked up from a level 1 to a level 7 by completing challenges, I built myself a little camp house by the river with a bed and made a crafting station for armor and cooking, even set up some turrets. You can store all your scrap in a vault-tech trunk at your camp AND anywhere you see a blue vault-tech trunk (in town or at a vendor) all your stuff is there! No more running back home to store all your junk. You just store it on the go. Then if you want move north or where-ever, you just pick up your entire camp "as is" and take it with you. No need to start all over again!

So...combat. Its numerous. Can be difficult at times until you get the hang of it. Even though I had a pipe gun very early on, I found it easier to use an axe, pitchfork, and hatchet. I died often when I first started but now I just run into combat with my fiery pitchfork and take out enemies with one hit. I feel like this game is similar to playing Fallout 4 in survival mode.

Other players: they are awesome, they are helpful, they are polite. We are all working toward the same goal. There are no griefers. As a level 3, I ran into another player who was ranked in the 100s, he was fantastic. We miked up and he gave me lots of tips, helped me out on a couple missions, made me a weapon and said that it was more fun for him to help out the lower ranked players and guide them through the game. Seriously! There is hope for humanity after all!

title: Weird design that doesn't quite know what it wants to be...
text:
Is this a space-saving and portable keyboard that includes a 10-key, or a full size chunky mechanical keyboard? Ultimately this keyboard tries to be both and therefor succeeds at neither of them.

Pros:
+Made from high quality materials, everything works seamlessly
+Bluetooth functionality works fine, seamlessly switching between 3 devices
+Full 10 key mechanical keyboard that is barely wider than a MBP

Cons:
- The keyboard feels cramped due to the layout
- Too chunky to be portable, negating the benefits of the smaller size.

At first glance, the compact layout is extremely appealing. There are several concessions made in order to get the entire 10 key layout into these dimensions. On the right side of the QWERTY keyboard, the shift, control, function and command keys are shrunk to make room for the left, up, and down arrow keys. For the 10-key, the "0" key is shrunk down from its normal larger size to be the same size as a standard key. Combine this with the 96% size of the rest of the keyboard, and the whole thing just feels cramped. Now this might be an acceptable concession for a keyboard that is intended to travel with you. However, the keyboard is THICK, and without some sort of snap on plastic cover I wouldn't want to throw it into a backpack or anything. Ultimately, this keyboard is too large to be a useful portable keyboard for most people and too cramped to be a convenient desktop keyboard.

title: Decent port of the 3DS classic
text:
Yes i said "classic" for a 3DS game...because this probably (aside from the obvious Mario entries) was the first 3rd party "classic" for the 3DS for me...and is still the optimum system to play it on in my opinion (withOUT a circle pad pro mind you!).

That stated, a lot was kept the same in this PS3 port, and that's both a good and bad thing. Good in that they didn't go ResEvil 6 and change a bunch of sequences to outdated Dragons Lair/God of War button mashing marathons. But bad in that, if you played the 3DS version, there isn't much left here to discover other than the slightly more textural graphics redefined for a bigger screen and...being able to play it on said bigger screen.

In the canon of Resident Evil games, the story gets pretty ridiculous...but that kind of became expected after Resident Evil 5 (and then furthermore after this came out, when ResEvil 6 was released). But the gameplay harkens back to somewhere between Resident Evil 4 and 5. You don't have to worry about toting around an artificial AI (for the most part)...there's a bit of strategy involved with upgrading your weapons, and you do need to shoot accurately and conserve ammo at times. But those looking for a massive amount of puzzles and creepy build of 0, CV, or 4 (let alone 1/2/3), might want to look elsewhere. The "thrills" aren't cheap like the car crashes and car chases of part 6. But the only go AS deep as "you better get some life and some bullets soon before you turn that corner and a hunter smacks you". Oh yeah spoiler alert, Hunters are back, and there's a lot of them at times!

Recommended for the longtime Resident Evil fan who got turned off by parts 5/6/OpRacoon City/whatever other offshoots in the series since 2007. But for those totally new, forget this and start with ResEvil 4...then work your way back...then come to this one. Then do 5 and 6.

title: So far, so good!
text:
It's only been about a week, but I'm very happy with this keyboard so far. I'm a writer who spends roughly eight hours a day, sometimes seven days a week at the keyboard. This one is responsive and gives me that satisfying click-clack this typewriter-training typist loves - some might find it annoying, though, and the space bar is particularly loud. That did throw me a bit at first.

I tried four different ergonomic setups with this before I found one that didn't result in hand fatigue: keyboard alone, both with the legs up and down, and then keyboard with wrist rest, legs both up and down. What finally worked for me was legs up and a wrist rest. I don't see this working without a wrist rest for any programmer or writer.

I'm also impressed with the battery life. I haven't recharged since I had it, though, granted I don't use the lights. I honestly didn't mean to let it go this long but I keep forgetting to plug it in at night despite the sticky note on my desk.

As other reviewers have mentioned, it's heavy. For me, that's a good thing because it doesn't slide around. I can't see traveling with it, though.

I also like the build. Unlike the last mechanical keyboard I had, which lasted only a couple of years, these keys are less gappy. That's perfect for someone with the unfortunate habit of eating at the desk no matter how many times I tell the kids to not do that because it trashes your keyboard. ;)

What would it take to make it a five for me? Probably a built-in wrist rest though, at this price point, I'm not complaining. I'm very happy with it.

As long as the dock is plugged into a power connection and the dock shield is plugged into the dock via USB, it will power on.

There is also a strobe light effect which quickly cycles through every color, which is mainly just to show off the dock shield. The dock shield likely uses very little electricity due to it being connected to USB and due to the lights being LEDs.

Do note that the face plates come with a film on them to protect them from scratches. You might have to use a finger nail to peel them off starting at the corners but they do come off. The protective film is likely to prevent scratching and fingerprints during the manufacturing / packing process.

considering how little content is in the actual game, its surprising how much enjoyment you can get out of this game. The game was basically cobbled together from the remains of "Project Titan", and it is a surprisingly well put together game considering how it came about.

title: Great fun and replay value
text:
Let me preface this by saying I've never understood the "minigame" concept. I've never played games like Super Smash Bros. before. In my GameCube days, a multiplayer game was something like Mario Golf, Mario Kart or Mario Tennis. I didn't really have any inclination to think I would enjoy Rayman Raving Rabbids, but I had been reading so many great reviews saying that this was THE game to get for the Wii.

So I picked it up, and it's probably my favorite Wii game right now. The biggest thing about it that I enjoy is the humor. Many of the games aren't particularly engaging by themselves, but the way they are presented to you is hilarious. The behavior and especially the sounds for the Rabbids are hysterical.

The single player game is in the format of a gladiatorial arena. In the opening sequence of the game, Rayman is captured by the Rabbids and thrown into a coliseum-like stadium in front of a crowd of jeering Rabbids. You're presented with five doors, one of which is locked until you beat at least three of the other challenges. The challenges generally fall into four categories ranging from precision (requiring you to have good control of the remote/nunchuk) to dancing (where you have to shake the controllers along with the beat of a song to inspire Rabbids to dance). If you beat three challenges, you unlock the middle door that leads to the "boss" level, which is usually either a shooter or a race. If you complete all four challenges, you also unlock a song or costume option. After you beat the "boss" level, you get "escorted" back to your cell where you can change costumes, listen to the music you've unlocked, review and replay the series of challenges you just played, and even plot your way out of the evil Rabbids' clutches.

Once you start completing challenges in the single-player game, you can go back to play them in a challenge mode to try and get the best score in a single-player mode or play up to 4 players in a variety of vs. or co-op modes. After each game in this mode, you're presented with a web code that you can enter at Ubisoft's Rayman website that enters you into the world rankings. My one gripe with this is, why doesn't the game simply contact the Rayman site directly if an internt connection is available? It's a big hassle to write down the code, then run into the other room where the computer is to enter the code. Luckily for me I have a laptop, so I can have the laptop open right next to me, but that's not always practical for everyone.

The minigames (and there are about 100 or more of them) themselves are generally very short... no more than 2-3 minutes or so for the longest ones, with some of them being under 15 seconds (though the shorter ones are typically the ones that require more control, so they're a bit harder, and you'll probably try them over and over again). Each one has a clever title, like "Bunnies don't know what to do with cows" on a mission where you have to twirl a cow above your head on the end of a chain and throw it for distance. Some of the games are actually physically exhausting... after playing a few of the missions your arms will feel like Jell-O.

For someone who originally had no interest in the "minigames" genre of video games, I really love this game. Whenever someone comes over or we take the Wii with us somewhere, we generally pull out Wii Sports first, just because it gives people a chance to get the hang of the Wii controllers, but then we switch to Rayman and the real fun begins.

What can I say that others haven't said? Nothing much, but F.E.A.R. 2 is a let down, and it's supposed to be a sequel. I was insulted on how dumbed-down the graphics, the gameplay and enemy AIs were. The graphics are what really ticked me off, although the original F.E.A.R. was not visually the best, but it was great for a 2005 game -- I managed to get 180fps on average with maxed settings, while F.E.A.R. 2 with it's watered downed graphics(also maxed out), I was locked at 60fps (without vsync). My specs are nowhere near high end, but I was surprised at this 60fps cap. If you played the first game, you can visually tell that F.E.A.R 2 is graphically inferior to that of the first game. Two other things that threw me off was the lack of mouse button support -- talk about a console port. A PC game made in 2009 does not support more than 3 mouse buttons!? Yes, F.E.A.R. 2 does NOT recognize your mouse's side buttons; If you want to program those buttons, you have to use 3rd party software to do so. Also there are no more quick saves, yup -- another step backwards. Your progress is saved via checkpoints.

Gameplay was disappointing as well. Leaning was completely removed; and of course they added the console "cover system", which doesn't help at all and I never once used. Story was surprisingly short. I was able to beat the game in under 8 hours without rushing the game. The scares weren't also that great, I was expecting some good ones, but was disappointed. As for multi-player, I wasn't able to play since I didn't want to make a GameSpy account.

Overall, F.E.A.R. 2 was not the game I was hoping for. It seems today, every FPS is a console port. I was hoping this wasn't a port, but it turned out to be with everything to the visuals to the gameplay, even the littlest thing was completely revamped for console systems. I don't recommend the game if you love F.E.A.R. and its expansion packs, this game is nothing like them. I give this game 2/5 stars; I saved it from the 1 start of death mainly because it's not one of the worst games I've played, but definitely one of my least favorite games.

title: Feed me, Seymour?
text:
I played through the first Halo and really enjoyed the single-player campaign. I never played the multiplayer game until I bought Halo 2.

Let's get this out of the way first: Halo 2's multiplayer is unparalleled. With a multitude of multiplayer games (Capture the Flag, Juggernaut, Team vs. Team, etc.) and a dizzying variety of terrains, there's plenty to keep Halo fans busy blowing each other up. The addition of the alien Elites as a playable character spice things up. You can also wield two weapons at a time, one in each fist, providing another combat option for those gunslingers that like their battles John Woo-style.

Unfortunately, Halo 2's single-player campaign is not as impressive. To whit, the alien Covenant's entire society is based on the idea that activating the giant rings throughout the universe (known as Halos) will put them on their journey of spiritual evolution. The reality is that Halo is a weapon designed to destroy the Flood, an infestation of aliens who turn human and alien alike into vicious zombies. And how do you keep the Flood from infecting every living thing? Why, by utterly destroying every living thing in the universe of course!

Play alternates between Master Chief and the alien elite known as the Arbiter. This gives the player both sides of the story, which is interesting...to a point. Eventually, the plot converges enough so that the two characters should really end up fighting each other. That would have been something, if the AI made you play through both battles from opposite sides by creating an enemy that uses your own moves.

But instead, about midway through the battle for the universe, a giant plant that looks like Audrey II from Little Shop of Horrors shows up. This planet, speaking in Jabba-esque guttural tones, rams the plot down our throats by grabbing the Arbiter and Master Chief and shoving them into opposite plot lines: the Arbiter ends up working with the humans, Master Chief ends up doing the alien dirty work.

Then things really get going, and just as Halo 2 hurtles towards the final battle on Earth...the game ends. I should have guessed something was up when, during E3 interviews about Halo 3, the CEO of Bungee only had this to say: "Are you ready to finish the war?" What he meant was, "Are you ready to finish the game you thought you were finishing in Halo 2?"

As you've probably noticed from my review of the second installment of Pirates of the Caribbean, I really, really, REALLY hate movies and games that fail to provide a whole story. It doesn't matter that this is part two of a three-part series. Writers and developers have an obligation to provide a full story; you CAN create a story with a beginning and end even though it's the middle of a series, as evidenced by The Two Towers.

Halo 2 is an improvement on the original, but it loses points for a weak campaign that forces you to play both sides, then throws in a talking plant to clean up the mess.

text:
Ok let me start by saying that this game is really fun but it does have some fatal flaws that you should look at before buying it.

The Pros:
-Good Campaign Story
-Brought Back and Revolutionized Zombies
-A lot of Extra Map Packs for Purchase
-A new and better lvling system in multiplayer
-A wide Range of Gun selection
-No more Noob-Tubing
-You can now Purchase your guns with money you earn rather than break your back with stupid achievements.
-You can Make your own Emblem
-Way better Killstreaks
-Improved Graphics
-Overall Very Fun!

The Cons:
-Campaign Gameplay is rather bland
-You'll lose connection to the game host more often
-Some Guns are not Accurately portrayed (Some Guns like M16 are 3 round bursts only and FAMAS is full auto only, also the AK47 is weaker than the M16?)
-They got rid of the SCAR

Overall you can plainly see that the Pros really outweigh the cons by A LOT! They have a storyline their just because but this really is a game that was made to shine for multiplayer and in fact in many ways I think it's much better than MW3 and MW2 and is a much more balanced and realistic gameplay. You get most of the most reputable guns of the cold war and even some rarely seen and unique ones! This is definatley a game your gonna want to pick up and try. The main reason I think people are dissapointed in this game is the same reason for most games/movies of this league.....OVER HYPE! Some people who gave this game a horrid rating do not have an open mind either to this style of gameplay or the reality of the design of this game. Is this game for everyone? No. But if you like fast paced action/first person shooters and like to interact with others than I highly urge you to give this game a go! Please note that if you do not have internet set up or dont like multiplayer games that you will HATE this game because it all revolves around human interaction for it's fun. If you like going solo go for Call of Duty 1,2,3, and World at War and maybe Call of Duty 4. And yes SCAR lovers I do feel your pain too. text:
I own a lot of mice- probably every mouse you could buy at Best Buy and a lot of up and coming mice companies' mice.

The clicks are awesome- well, the main mouse 1 and mouse 2 clicks. The clicks are sturdy and satisfying. The side mouse buttons are alright. Nothing special, but not noticeably worse than other other mouse I use. The scroll wheel... this ones tough. Basically, the actual scroll is one of the best I've experienced. It's smooth but tactile enough to be pleasant and discernable, but the click of the scroll wheel takes a noticeable amount of force. Like, I really have to think about it when I push the thing down. It's a big reason that the mouse isn't my main mouse.
Lastly, the cable is ok. It looks cool on the retro version of the mouse, but it's heavy and it is felt whenever I move the mouse, even in a bungee.

TLDR;
Great M1 and M2 clicks
Passable side button clicks
Tough scroll wheel click but satisfying scroll
Great feet
Good shell shapes with a bit of creak over time
Cable is... ok. Bungee helps but it's still weighty compared to the mouse

title: IMHO, It's Either a Das or a Matais If You Want a Mechical Keyboard
text: Computer users searching for the next best thing in mechanical keyboards will undoubtedly take a gander at models made by Das and Matais, two top makers. I have keyboards of each brand, both selling for about $125. There's this one, for my Mac Pro (with Cherry MX Blue keyswitches) and the Matais Tactile Pro 4 (with Alps keyswitches) for my PC. I bought the Matais several  months back and liked it so much, that I set out to buy the equivalent model for my Mac, Pro with the Mac-specific keys. However, I didn't like the look of the Matais Tactile Pro in Apple-style white. All the keys were cluttered with two or three icons or letters and the whole thing just looked too messy. I guess the Steve Jobs design ethos has worn off on me. I'll add Matais says its Mac keyboard is very similar to the famed Apple extended keyboard from years back. If you remember and like that keyboard, you'll probably like the Tactile Pro. I'd read good things about the Das, so I decided to try it. My verdict? I give the Matais a slight edge, based on personal preference for the feel of the switches and not the features or quality of the keyboard, which are first rate. These are solidly built keyboards and I think most typists would be happy with either brand. I was as a journalist for more than 30 years and I know a good keyboard when I pound on one. I used to love the fat chunky keyboard that came with my earliest Mac, IBM's early keyboard and the Atex newspaper publishing system keyboards, but I'm getting off track. As noted, the Das uses Cherry MX switches and the Matais uses Alps switches. You'll have to do your own research to learn about the nitty-gritty differences among switches, but here's what I noticed: The Matais is more "clicky." You have to give the keys a good poke to trigger a response. The Das keyboard action is slightly softer and you don't have to tickle the keys with the same commitment because they're not as springy and don't travel quite as far as the Matais, from what I can tell. The difference in keystroking is noticeable but not dramatically so. If you like to bang away on a keyboard and you enjoy the clackety-clack sound it makes, you'll like the Matais Alps switches. Don't get me wrong, the Das Cherry switch also has a nice feel and I guess that's what most mech keyboard buyers go for. And it's a wee bit quieter so you might prefer that if you're in an open office where noise levels might be an issue. The Das has two USB ports on the side and a cable with two USB plugs on the end, so keep that in mind if you're low on USB ports. It also might make a difference to some people: The letters on the Das are all lower case. I like the crisp unknown-to-me font the maker uses on the keys. All in all, I'm tempted to send this one back and try the Tactile Pro 4, despite its ugly looks.

title: Just what I needed for game sounds & Discord chat
text:
I still can’t believe the Nintendo Switch doesn’t support Bluetooth headphones out of the box … it seems like such a no-brainer. Especially for a console that has the draw of being able to take it anywhere and game!

I play my Switch in handheld mode 99.9% of the time, and usually play with the sound off 99.9% of the time so as not to bug anyone else in the house. When I play co-op games with friends and use Discord for voice chat, I have to keep my sound off then too, because I can’t hear everything. Splatfest is just not as fun without music, and how am I supposed to hear a shooting star in Animal Crossing??

I mention all of this to say that the HomeSpot Bluetooth Adapter Pro is *exactly* what I needed. The adapter allows me to pair my Switch, headphones, and phone so that I can listen to game sounds *and* be able to chat on Discord or listen to music on my phone.

The instructions are clear and easy to understand. It took me about 3 minutes to connect my Switch, headphones, and phone. Now I enjoy playing on my Switch even more because I can hear game music and sounds!

The Bluetooth adapter can also be used in docked mode. The box includes a USB-C to USB-A Adapter to connect it to the dock.

I love the form factor. The adapter plugs in flush against the bottom of the Switch. Some adapters stick out a lot, but this one is small. I’m currently using a Satisfye grip, which adds a bit of length to the Joycons, so I can rest my Switch on my lap or stomach and not have the weight of it resting on the adapter.

The only thing I am disappointed about is that the adapter doesn’t support pass through charging. The description doesn’t say that it does, but I personally didn’t realize I wouldn’t be able to charge my switch while using it. I just wanted to mention that for anyone else who might not realize.

title: The most popular and accessible MOBA game
text:
First, I wouldn't recommend buying the box. You can download the game for free from Riot Games, so there isn't really any need to pay for the software unless you are dead-set on collecting the box as a collector's item or something like that.

----

League of Legends (LoL) is the largest (in terms of players) game of its genre -- the "Multiplayer Online Battle Arena" genre of game, or "MOBA". The first MOBA was Defense of the Ancients (DOTA), which originated as a player-made modification (mod) to the real-time strategy (RTS) game Warcraft III. Lots of acronyms, because this neck of the gaming community is very acronym-heavy. The idea of an RTS is to collect resources and build a base, with structures to create and upgrade various units, and then use these units to defeat the enemy generally by destroying its base. Warcraft III introduced the concept of having "hero" units which would be present from the start of a game, and would have various abilities to help the other basic units, and sometimes battle the enemy's hero unit(s). The DOTA mod sought to remove from Warcraft III the entire dynamic of collecting resources and building a base, and replace it with a larger number of heroes competing over a map with preset structures. So while the basic idea of the game has its roots in the RTS genre, it doesn't play really like an RTS at all, but is essentially its own genre of game.

What does that look like? In a MOBA game, generally five players are teamed up against another five players. Each player controls a hero character (known in LoL as a "Champion"). Each champion (LoL has something like 102 of them now and periodically releases new ones) has a unique set of abilities, and is designed to play a specific "role" on a team. In this area, there is some variety between different MOBA games, but in LoL, champions are generally either physical melee damage dealers, ranged magical damage dealers, ranged physical damage dealers, tanks, or support (buff/heal/scout). Each champion has four abilities (the Q, W, E and R abilities) which get upgraded during the course of a match as the champion increases from level 1 to level 18 (which is the cap in any given match). In addition, there are two "summoner spells" that the player selects before the match begins which are more situations (teleports, blinks, situational damage spells) with longish cooldowns. Champions upgrade their abilities by gaining levels and, especially for certain kinds of champions which scale in power much more by acquiring items, by using the gold gained by last-killing the enemy's minions (known as creeps) to purchase upgrades at the store at the team base. Gold is awarded to a champion only if the champion deals the killing blow (the "last hit") to a creep, so the skill of "last hitting" is critical for most champions in the game (other than support champions, who generally seek to avoid last hitting so that the other players can raise more gold and upgrade themselves as a priority for the team).

All five on five MOBA games have a very similar map (LoL has three-player maps as well, but most games are played on the familiar 5 vs. 5 map). The map has the enemy bases at opposite corners (southwest and northeast) and three pathways between the bases (known as the top, mid, and bot (for bottom) lanes). Each lane has turrets located on it which attack champions for a lot of damage, and which must be destroyed to advance along the lane to the enemy base. Each base has turrets and structures in it which must similarly be destroyed before the enemy base itself, known as the nexus, can be attacked and destroyed -- the team to first kill its opponents nexus wins the match. Between the lanes is a series of wooded areas with winding pathways through them referred to as the "jungle" -- it contains monsters that can be killed for gold and XP gains of varying difficulty. There is also a river running through the middle of the map, roughly from northwest to southwest, which intersects with all three lanes and forms the border between each team's side of the map. There are two "super" monsters located along this river which can be killed by a team for a substantial bonus.

During the course of the game, each team's base spawns creeps at a regular pace, which automatically march down each lane towards the enemy base, attacking enemy creeps and turrets along the way. The course of the game generally takes place in phases, with the initial phase consisting of "laning", which is essentially when players in the lanes will be trying to last hit the enemy's creeps (for gold gains) while simultaneously interfering with the enemy player(s) trying to do the same thing - something which is known as "harassing" - without generally pushing into the other team's side of the river very much. Of course, players will also be trying to kill other players during this phase as well, but there is a greater emphasis on acquiring gold to upgrade the champion gear as quickly as possible, while gaining levels and ability upgrades. Around the middle of the game, the focus tends to shift towards "pushing", which involves moving onto the enemy's side of the river, destroying the enemy's turrets, and eventually pushing into the enemy base to destroy its structures (which results in your side spawning much tougher creeps) and eventually win the game by destroying its nexus. From the mid-phase of the game on, the focus tends to shift to team fights where one team tries to eliminate a good portion of the enemy team at one time so as to make advances quickly while they are on a respawning/dead timer and not active in the game. Games generally take at least 30 minutes, and can last 45 to 60 minutes depending on the players involved.

LoL is the most accessible of the MOBA games because it has been designed with streamlined mechanics in many areas as compared with other DOTA-type games. So the game is easier to get into than its competitors, which is likely why it has grown to the enormous size that it has (something like 14 million players per month and over a million playing at any one time). If you have never played a MOBA game before, it's a good place to start.

In terms of competition, the main competitors are DOTA itself (which is a mod for Warcraft III and requires Warcraft III to play), DOTA 2 (currently in beta, and which will not require Warcraft III to play) and Heroes of Newerth (HoN). Both DOTA/DOTA2 and HoN are smaller, with a more hardcore (and more rough) community than LoL's and are considered to be (and frankly just are) unfriendly for new players - you will get yelled at, cursed at, belittled and so on with ferocity and regularity in these games by more advanced players, so best advised to have a very thick internet skin before wading into those pools. The DOTA games and HoN both have somewhat less streamlined mechanics in several areas (some of which the DOTA/DOTA2 and HoN players specifically prefer to LoL's mechanics) such as (1) the ability to "deny" the XP and gold gain for one's enemies in the lane/farm phase by killing friendly creeps before the enemy does, thereby starving the enemy of gold for advancement and upgrades), (2) the use of a player-controlled courier for ferrying gear upgrades from the shop to the player rather than LoL's instant return to base mechanic, (3) the absence of stealth bushes present in LoL (places players can hide from attack), and (4) an embracing of relative lack of balance with several overpowered abilities by design (whereas LoL tries to balance these out of the game). When Riot Games created LoL, two principal ideas of the design were to avoid things that they considered to be "anti-fun", as well as experiences which emphasized "the burden of knowledge". In general, this has meant making the game more accessible, avoiding abilities which are so overpowered that they one-shot a player who doesn't already know to stay away from the other player due to knowing the abilities of the other player inside-out, balancing champions/heroes in a relative sense and the like. It is, however, a major source of disagreement within the MOBA community, and the main dividing line between the fans of LoL and the fans of many of the other games in the genre. Another new MOBA called "SMITE" developed by Hi-Rez studios is currently in closed beta testing, and incorporates some of the more entry-friendly aspects of LoL with a third person perspective (rather than the more common isometric "top down" perspective in other MOBA games, including LoL), which may also be worth a look for players new to the MOBA genre.

Having said that, LoL itself has a significant learning curve (even if, by comparison, the other MOBA games pretty much have a nearly vertical learning cliff), and also a fairly rough community (although much less so than the DOTA games and HoN). It's generally the place to get started with these kinds of games, but expect to spend quite a bit of time reading guides and looking at videos if you wish to improve your game, as well as a lot of practice with certain mechanics such as last-hitting. These are games meant to be played competitively for years on end, and will repay that investment if you are willing to make it, and even LoL, which is relatively more accessible, is still not generally designed as a game you will do well in if you just play casually every once and a while.

title: Don't Waste Yo' Time on Hillbilly Trash
text:
Played this at a friend's house. We sampled our way through this lame game. First there's the main line of play and that's when you take on the character of Willie's son John-Luke. You have perform certain quests to become a full-fledged Duckman. Quests like playing pranks on your family at the Office, racing Fan Boats in the Swamps, Catchin' Frogs, and Callin' Ducks with the Family's Famous Duck Calls. There's even a strange quest where you have to search for your Uncle Si's lost treasures with a metal detector. And those treasures can be from the usual to the bizarre. When I go detectin' I find coins, rings, beer and soda-pop cans, bottle caps, pull-tabs, rusty nails, and hopefully lockboxes. Lockboxes are always interesting 'cause you never know what you'll find hidden away. Could be lots of coins, jewelry, money, or maybe those family secrets they've been keeping all these years - like what's been in the news these past few years; especially child molestation, preaching hate, and you have to wonder why Phil does that; perhaps Phil and Si had a bit of explorin' with the other when they were teens.

Gameplay - the usual, but I get tired of hearin' these good ol' boys draggin' they lines like dey nevuh went fer schoolin'. It gits old. And it's stupid. The races are fun, but over fast. Then there's the killing of frogs, which I do not condone. Bullfrogs are a part of the swamp's overall ecology. They are put of nature's food chain, helping control insect populations, and in turn are food for large birds and reptiles (like snakes). Frogs don't hurt anyone, nor the environment. Sure they might have tasty legs, but Duck's are too.

Overall - it's stupid. Plus it appears that the game was created just to make money off the television show's many fans. Created a bit too quickly me thinks. This could have been a much better game if they had concentrated on the Family Business and Ducking Calling and Hunting. But how can you make an entertaining game out of that? Instead they built a game on hillbilly tasks, and it makes you wonder why a multimillionaire family dynasty would rather do that (the hillbilly way), then spend their money on the real thing. A Hillbilly Waterpark? Take you kids to a real one; you can afford it. A vacation at home? Take your family to Orlando and it's world famous Amusement Parks; you can afford it. And lastly, when you think about how they're portrayed in the game as your every day backwoods Bible toting, Jesus lovin' family, preaching God's good will by setting an example, you have to wonder why Phil preaches hate in his spare time.

title: These are a hard pass for me...
text:
I purchased these with high hopes but was horribly let down. Plugging in via on-board (both front case and main back) they sounded weak and tinny. Plugging in via my Sound Blaster Z, the powered boost helped in terms of volume, but the lack of substance / tinny undertone was now even more dominant.

Going even further, I plugged them into a GoXLR to utilize even more of a 'boost', still tinny. My XLR makes a $15 headset from Walmart sound amazing, it did no justice here. I even went as far as purchasing a USB adaptor in one last effort to know for sure that it wasn't a lack of power to the unit, it's just the quality of the speakers, still tinny / no substance.

The default leatherette ear pads are comfortable, but cheap feeling and I could tell that they would crumble over time because it's the 'thin' material that just flakes when they dry out OR get overused. Because of this, I did purchase Felt earpads (search for Genuine Sennheiser HZP 26 Replacement Ear Pads Cushions). They fit beautifully and made the unit more comfortable, this did not assist with the sound, if anything made it worse because your ear was no longer 'locked' into the leather, so they were swapped back to the original pads.

I'm not looking for headphones that will rattle my eardrums, by any means, but having absolutely no substance on any song listened to, or game played, just takes away from the overall experience, especially on the higher end of $150. An audiophile would absolutely hate these, and the sound issues (no matter having an EQ adjustment or flat) caused issues in-game where I didn't hear any footsteps for anything going on around me. In an FPS it's essential to know your surroundings, no settings anywhere on my PC allowed for this without having to full crank these to 100% on both the computer AND the headset. I wish I could give these less than a 1 star, but Amazon doesn't allow for it.

I've already started the return process on these, really unfortunate. I'll continue my search for something better.

title: A micro-managers dream come true
text:
This game was recommended to me by a friend who also loves real time simulation games. Next to the Simcity franchise, this is one of the most popular and well-received RTS games out there.

A little backstory... I started playing Sim Theme Park (1999) back in 2000. That was (and still is) a very fun simulation game. One of the best in my opinion. I feel the mixture of real-world accuracy and fun gameplay (even though very cartoony) was executed perfectly by the developers. Furthermore, the overall aesthetics and art style of the game are very appealing to me.

RT3, however, is a jumbled, overly-complicated mess in my opinion. The UI does not flow well, and the item menu layout makes it difficult to manage your park. Most importantly, there are just way too many options to play with! Everything (and person) in the park has a full-range of options to tweak... enough to make an OCD person go absolutely nuts, lol. I fully support real-world accuracy in these games, but I also understand that it's still a game, and I want to have fun playing it. And the developers definitely went full-tilt making RT3 as realistic as possible. Some people will no doubt love this, but I think that most people coming from Simcity or Sim Theme Park will find the game far too micro-manage-y.

The sandbox mode is fun, but since money is not involved, you quickly lose motivation playing it. What's the point if you can build anything you want, immediately? The campaign mode is not what I expected... I was thinking it was more along the lines of Sim Theme Park or Simcity where you start with a lump sum of money and an empty park, and you build your park from there, managing it along the way to keep a positive cash flow. Instead, the campaigns are somewhat preformed, giving you a basic park that you 'take-over' management of. Not very exciting in my opinion.

Overall, the game is not as fun as I had hoped for. If they allowed users to let the park run more autonomously (perhaps an 'auto-pilot' mode if you will) with the ability to tweak various items if needed, that would be better. Or, as an alternative, provide advice to the user on various aspects of the game (i.e. people find admission prices very cheap... people are not satisified with the quality of ice cream offered... etc). In it's current state, however, I don't want to go through my 5 hot dog stands and adjust the amount of mustard on my hot dogs.... and have to guess what the best selling price would be based on the insignificant amount of financial data the game provides real-time. The concept is great, but they just strayed too far in to the weeds without providing enough framework to allow the player to adequately adjust all of the options.

Those coming from Simcity- or Sim Theme Park-style games beware... you probably won't enjoy this one.

title: This is a rare, perfect game.
text:
Let me start by saying that I don't even like Space Invaders. The 1978 classic was before even my time, and the lack of sophistication always turned me away. When Space Invaders Extreme came out in 2008, however, I was attracted to the colorful and chaotic yet retro presentation, and decided to buy the game on a whim. It surpassed any expectations I could have reasonably had, and SIE quickly became one of my favorite games on the DS thanks to its creative use of sound, unique soundtrack, pseudo-retro graphics, and amazing challenge.

A little over one year later, a sequel was released exclusively for the DS, and wanting more invader goodness, I hastily purchased a copy on release day. I would have been happy with just more of the same. Instead, it absolutely DESTROYED my expectations, and improved on the original in every conceivable way - more enemies, better bosses, better music, better scoring system, better leveling system, even harder challenges, and better difficulty balance with no more "cheap" deaths. SIE2 is so great...so satisfying, challenging, and well thought out, that for the first and only time in my life, I chased the global leaderboards (I got in the top 10 in three out of four). It's the kind of game that should satisfy everyone...there is that intense, high speed pressure that you only find in arcade games, yet the extremely sophisticated scoring system requires you to keep a cool head and plan every move as you play. The system is incredibly flexible, and works just as well for time trials as it does for high scores. Even if you don't care about leaderboards and simply want to make a run through each path, the variety of enemies, stages, and increasing difficulty will satisfy. It is so good that I went out the next week and bought several extra copies to distribute to my friends.

title: Play it your first time around the block
text:
A lot of people say this is the greatest game in the series. It seems a lot of "impartial" game review magazines and Web sites say the same thing. I can't judge if this is hype or if it's just me, though.

First off, I do not fault the graphics like so many people do. Those who do fault it for this reason are not true gamers. A good game transcends its own graphics. I've said before, even if a game was 8-bit, as long as the story was enthralling, I'd be fine. A real gamer recognizes that aspect.

However, there's a lot of this game that is bad. On to the gist of the review.

A friend of mine has faulted this game as "Final Anime." Truly, it did take on a lot of anime-esque themes and character personalities. I use Cloud as an example. He never grows as a character from the start of the game to the end. No, he doesn't. Get over it. He is the same brooding, emo kid at the end of the game that he was when it started. Not to mention, there's a "huge" reveal about his backstory on disc 2 that's reminiscent of anime, where it diverts from the main story for episodes and episodes and does. not. die. Not to mention, the excessive flashbacks, which, I know are not new to the series, which just play up how underdeveloped the characters are.

Onto the gameplay. Each character is completely indistinguishable from the others. The only differences are pixel sets and limit breaks. Magic should be based on class. In this game, every character can equip any kind of magic. Stats are so similar between characters who are supposed to be fighters and those who are supposed to be mages. There's no distinction between them. The materia system cripples the game because anyone can be a healer or a status magic user.

Sephiroth. Most definitely not the coolest villain in the series. People think he's cool because he walked through fire with a huge effing sword. That does not equate to cool. You want a good villain? Go with FF6's Kefka. He actually DID destroy the world and created a religion unto himself.

I fault the character development the most in this game. No one grows. No, they don't. Deal with it. Real character development can be found with characters from FF6 like Locke Cole. He swears to himself he will never let the fate of his fiancee Rachel fall upon any of his friends.

Also, Aeris isn't the first main character in the series to die. That goes to FF5's Galuf.

Give the game a shot if you're an RPG newbie. It might hold you for a repeat, but it also might not. Take this game with a grain of salt. I own it for completion's sake.

title: Works well for large hands, right hand claw grip
text:
I have been using this mouse on my production machine for 7-8 hours a day for a while now, and I like the form factor, smooth glide and responsive buttons. If you use the Logitech software, it is almost absurdly configurable. I also liked the LMB and RMB click feel which was very positive and not mushy. The click wheel also has the same firm click feel. You can easily switch to click-free scrolling with a press of button on the top. I tried it for a while, it was nearly friction free (but not my cup of tea- I like the clicks).

Set-up was easy. The box and set-up instructions are clear and straight forward. You need to download the software from the Logitech site, but if you have been using high end gaming mouses for a while you are probably used to that. However, Windows 7 recognize the mouse without the software if you want to forgo the download (and lose the customization).

One neat touch is the braided mouse cable, which doesn't seem to get hung up on stuff as much as the cables on cheaper mouses. Another is the well formed right thumb groove, which felt great in use. Overall, this is a fantastic corded gaming mouse with a ton of adjustments (weight, button configurations, DPI ect) that works well for right handed claw grips. Recommended.

title: Better than Elements, but still not great
text:
Heroes Chronicles: Clash of the Dragons follows the adventures of Tarnum, a former barbarian lord leading an elf king's army against the united forces of Mutare and her dragon minions. Just as in the companion game, Heroes Chronicles: Masters of the Elements, heroes are developed, quests performed, monster armies recruited and castles and territories expanded as the hero tries to fend off invading forces.

Terrain varies from sylvan to rocky to positively infernal and creatures match their homelands, ranging from flame-throwing demons, unicorns and battle centaurs to dragons of all types. Magic items, supplies and even spells can be bought or traded. Fundamental to success is establishing different types of strongholds that generate creatures of varied ability. The game uses the same engine as Heroes Chronicles: Masters of the Elements and gameplay revolves around adventurers leading troops, thus causing them to act more as "mules" to transport troops than heroic entities.

Combat can be tedious, though battles compared to those in Masters of the Elements are a bit more even. There are fewer "death-trap" scenarios, although they still occasionally crop up. Some unique conditions modify each scenario, such as rescuing a particular character or performing a quest to give you an edge in completing the mission.

Unfortunately, the game engine is somewhat flawed and the same problems that plague Masters of the Elements are evident here. The most glaring error is the separation of NPCs in the plot and as adventurer's in the game. It's possible to have a significant adventurer from the storyline die during gameplay, yet the narrative blithely ignores the event. Conversely, an adventurer can be kidnapped in the plot line but still be leading troops in the game. Ultimately, these inconsistencies destroy the impact of the storyline.

A good example of an inconsistency revolves around Tarnum's concern for Valita, a potential spy in his army. As part of a major subplot, the concern should be ill founded since, after all, you control Valita as an adventurer. Unfortunately, what happens to her has no impact on her role in the plot, as she can die and the plot continues as if she were still alive.

The end conditions for each scenario can almost always be solved through brute force alone, which detracts from the appeal of the entire adventure. It's even possible to resolve the ending without actually fighting the main villain. While Heroes Chronicles: Clash of the Dragons is an improvement over Masters of the Elements, it can't overcome the flaws of the game design.

title: Confused game, bad controls
text:
This game is a hybrid of games we've all played before but it makes for an overall confused experience because of that. It is an interesting idea to take the best games and sort of mix them up though. It's got the focus button and combat cover system of Gears of War along with RPG elements in it and button mashing/timed events too.

I'm not a big fan of the "mic" commands interface since I don't have a mic on my computer it makes for an awkward unnecessary element in my mind. I'm forced to push the tab button and then select a command with the F button all while trying to blast the bad guys. Trying to pick the right comment to get what you want out of teammates is more of a tedious chore than any fun and their usually phlegmatic responses don't improve it. Having to watch for the comment button to move forward I guess forces you to be attentive. Even if I did have a mic button it's just too weird to talk to myself out loud while I'm playing a game. Hope they drop this part if there is a second game.

Also this is just not a PC game, it's really an afterthought port. It's painfully evident from the first time you start the game. The controls are default Xbox control mapped. Once you change the settings to mouse/keyboard(MKB) it's another painful surprise that the mapping seems odd. Spacebar and F are the enter and exit as well as action buttons with the mouse being standard point/shoot. I wish they could have done more work with the mouse wheel/wheel buttons as far as switching weapons, etc.

As far as combat it's pretty standard GOW stuff, cover, shoot etc. I wish there was the option to use the grenade as a separate button as it is you have to use 1234 to switch to grenade throw it then switch back to your shooter. The weapons are pretty standard which is disappointing in such a futuristic game a bit of imagination there would have been nice.

There are too many cut scenes in this game, thankfully they had the good sense to make them largely optional. It feels like you are just watching a CG movie, 3-4 cut scenes in one long sequence.

This game could have been much better but there are too many elements that take away from the flow of the action, which is what this game is at heart: an action game. The RPG elements via the command menu are unnecessary to me and poorly executed. When not in combat the character interactions/interaction menu is uninteresting and annoying. The whole trust system via making the right comments and actions is another unnecessary.

Graphics are pretty standard, nothing spectacular but nothing terrible.

I wouldn't recommend this at it's current price, if you can wait until there is a sale or simply wait a month or two and get it when it's at the correct price: 20 bucks or less.

title: Amazing Detailed Wonderful Game!
text: I picked up Breath of the Wild the day it was released and am still playing the game (attempting to find all Korok Seeds). There are still places I am discovering on the map even after facing Ganon that are new, simply unexplored from before. The ability to switch the controls was very useful as the default for run, jump, attack were in odd positions for me that didn't make doing all of those at once very easy. There were only a few glitches that I picked up on, but these didn't take away from the game play at all.  1) Hitting a Guardian with an arrow and it falls into the ground and vanishes. I don't know how or why this happens but it happened a few times during game play.  2) Non registered horse (temperament wild) would run into a mountain. Literally, inside of the mountain. Link would be thrown off of the horse, but the horse would keep going.--- Please know these instances didn't happen often and by no means took away from game play once again. The change from Skyward Sword to this game is worth the wait. If you are new to this series or have been playing it across thirty years, you will not find a game more worth your dollars than Breath of the Wild. The open world truly lets you go at your own pace. Oh, and there's no annoying side kick/Navi/Fi. It's been well over a decade since I've played a video game that I've come to enjoy this much and the replay value is pretty high. Looking forward to download content in the summer and winter.

title: can I have half my money back please?
text:
I might be spoiled by Amazon's 6.99 downloads, because after finishing this game within a week of purchasing it I don't feel like it's a good value at all. Of course, this is comparing it to same-priced games like Burger Shop 2 and Monarch the Butterfly King, games that not only suck you in but are able to provide enough game to keep you playing for weeks straight. Pure Hidden is fun, it's not addicting to me because I don't find picture-find games addicting, but it is a game that I've enjoyed playing. The scenes which hide the pictures are different than what you find in a typical picture find game. The main pictures are gorgeous. I would even say they are works of art that one might frame and put on their wall. They aren't basic scenes with images of items cut out and scattered all over the place, rather they are well thought out and designed to cleverly hide the items within them, making them quite challenging. So far I've had to use the cheat tool to find at least one of the items in almost all of the scenes.

Unfortunately, I feel like the overall setup of the game was a total miss. Working to complete your gallery of scenes that you have finished (which you can install as a desktop background after you do) has nice appeal, but there is A LOT of filler in between the picture-find scenes, which consists of mini-games and mini-puzzles, some of which are completely pointless. For example, the "decorate your bathroom" activity--this one shows up multiple times as a "mini-game" but each time you're only given an option of one item to be put in a predetermined place, and ding, you're done for that one and it moves you on to the next puzzle. Totally pointless. Some of the mini-games have a really neat concept, like bursting the bubbles to play a song, but there is no goal whatsoever, and after about 15 seconds you get bored after realizing there's no challenge to it and hit next to move on, which you could have done in the first 5 seconds of the mini-game. A few of the mini-games are implemented with some really innovative ideas, like the "find the difference games" where you use your mouse to turn the 3D image and look at it from all sides. Now if there had been more of these in place of the pointless mini-games, then I think Pure Hidden would have been much more fulfilling. Unfortunately, Pure Hidden seemed to end as soon as it started. Overall, if you have 6.99 to spend and you're trying to find a game that will keep you engaged for more than a week, keep looking. Amazon has tons of 6.99 game downloads that last an eternity compared to this one.

title: A fantastic system
text:
I have so many great things to say about this system, and very few negatives. Nintendo has done a fantastic job updating the 3DS line and correcting some of the previous problems that older versions had.

The biggest to me is the eye tracking with the 3D feature. My husband has an older and smaller 3DS and the 3D feature doesn’t work as well. It’s a strain on the eyes after a while because it doesn’t stay in focus correctly. With the New 3DS I don’t have that problem at all and can play games for hours in 3D mode without issue. It will go out of focus when I move and shift around, but the infrared kicks on and adjusts it quickly.
Another one of my favorite changes, albeit small, is the slight re-positioning of the buttons downward. It’s not a lot, but it’s enough that the console feels more comfortable in my hands for longer play sessions.

My biggest gripe with this system is how quickly the battery drains in sleep mode. Ideally you’ll want to leave it in sleep mode when you’re not using it so that you can Streetpass with it, but mine only lasts 2-3 days in sleep mode before it needs a charge. It’s not a huge problem by any means, but it’s a little frustrating to take it out of my backpack and find it dead.

Another minor complaint is how small the SD card is that it ships with. Save yourself the headache and just buy a larger card with the system and immediately upgrade it. There’s nothing more frustrating than wanting to download that big beautiful new game and finding that you can’t because your SD card is full.

Overall though this system is great. It has lots of options for games to suit all tastes, a good and steady 3D display, good play-time battery life and a bunch of fun quirky features (like augmented reality) to bring out the childlike wonder in anyone.

title: Turn all the lights off at night, I dare you.
text:
Ok the only thing that can sum up this game is as follows: Psychologically Damaging. I must say I've never been this afraid of a game. I've played all the Resident Evil games and I must say they were cake walks compared to this one (although I must say after a half-hour, RE lost its ability to scare me... even alone in my apartment with the lights off).
The big difference here is that in RE is dealing with corporeal things... sure they may be around corners or jump at you suddenly from the ceiling/window/grave/etc, but they are still just zombies. In the end they still have to come at you and you've got a nice arsenal of weapons waiting for them.
Fatal Frame is much different in that regard. In FF you deal with the ethereal, things that can appear and disappear at whim, and don't need to open a door to go through it. The worst part is that all you have to defend yourself with is a camera... which means in order to take out one of these specters, you have to stare the thing directly in the face first.
If you are looking for something to make you jump out of your pants, this probably isn't the game you're looking for. This game has a much meaner style to it. It simply heaps on the psychological trauma gradually, so that when you are done playing a session you feel emotionally drained, and not in any kind of condition to go to bed.
Aside from the high horror factor this game totes, it's also beautifully done. The ambient music and sounds set the mood perfectly, and the scenery is masterful. The setting of an old Japanese village is well picked, and the rendering of the village itself is superb. The only problem is that sometimes doors are a little hard to see, but that is mostly because I wasn't used to looking for sliding doors. Plus had there been western style doors, the setting would not have looked authentic.
The big hiccup for this game is the dual character setup. While you can move at a mild pace, not fast mind you, your partner takes up the rear with a horrible limp and no speed to go with it.
So all in all I would recommend this game. But for those of you expecting Resident Evil, I suggest you rent it first. This game is obviously not for everyone.

title: It's OK as DLC
text:
This is a _very_ short campaign. Before going into the campaign itself:

Installation was much easier than installing the original game. Probably due to the fact that, by now, you have the Origin client installed, and the DLC installs thru that. Once installed, it does NOT show up on the main list of games, and the order receipt shows "no serial number necessary", so it was a little confusing at first how to actually PLAY the DLC. It doesn't appear in the main menu under "Downloadable content".

Once the DLC is installed, you "Continue" an existing game, and you'll trigger a new quest to start playing the DLC. You have to be level 10 to trigger the quest, but if you've finished the OC, you should more than meet the requirements. This is rather an interesting method to activate the DLC, and I liked it.

I was level 40 (the max), have most of my skills maxxed, and a nicely outfitted character who migrated right into the DLC campaign.

This said, consider the rest of this review to contain possible spoilers.

As I said, the DLC campaign is very short, and most of it revolves around building your new keep, which is a very sweet residence indeed, a miniature town. In between running the restoration quests, you complete the main story quests for Dead Kel, as many of these quests will intersect. So you'll be in the area anyways.

One word of warning, and a definite spoiler, once you begin the final Dead Kel quest, going into his dungeon, make sure you have enough inventory space to loot every chest and pile, because once you vanquish Dead Kel, it looks like you cannot return.

I didn't log how many hours I played until I defeated Dead Kel, but it was certainly less than 10, and probably something you can hammer out over a weekend. As I said above, since I was maxxed out on character, at no point in playing did I get that "oh crap" feeling, where I was in over my head. That's kind of unfortunate, and as annoying as it is to reload an earlier save, it's all part of the challenge.

Playing a game is not always about rushing to the end, and in this DLC, there are ongoing quests you can keep playing. These are similar to the "tasks" in the OC, and entail you talking to some of the denizens of your new castle, as you dispense justice or take on other challenges.

I have not tried to go back to the mainland of the OC, but I do know you cannot fast-travel to e.g. Rathir, so I don't know if there is a method to return...

There was no increase to the level cap, it's still level 40, and I really didn't find any loot that exceeded what I already had, save a few pieces of armor. I did miss some of the chests, so I'll go back and loot everything I can.

title: Great when new, but it won't last.
text: This was a great joystick when I first got it.  The buttons are good, springs were good, the software is pretty good, physically it's very sturdy and it feels solid.  The problems started after a few months of use.  I started getting dead spots, drift and it sometimes didn't return to center in the games I played (physically it was centered, but the flight sim didn't think it was.) The bottom line is that by using pots (old style variable resistors) instead of Hall Effect sensors this joystick has a limited lifespan.  When the pots wear out or get dirty it's done.  I'd say 1 year of heavy use is a good estimate.  You simply can't expect pots to last too long when you are constantly moving them for hours a day.  They are really meant for occasional adjustment to volume and such in radios and TVs not for being hammered by continuous movement in a joystick.  Hall Effect sensors don't suffer this problem because there is no physical contact between the moving parts.  They use magnetic induction to determine the stick position.  So, save yourself some money and get a Hall Effect joystick like the Thrustmaster T-16000M Flight Stick or go big and get an all metal one like Thrustmaster Hotas Warthog, Replica Split Throttle System.  I'm not pushing Thrustmaster, but they seem to be the only company selling Hall Effect sticks now that Microsoft isn't making joysticks anymore.

The controls are a nightmare, Just to get this animal to walk where you want it to walk at any sort of speed is disastrous. It’s “open world” in a very small way. Get used to dying again, and again.
The graphics are ok I guess, I mean who plays this for the beauty of it? It’s an idea thrown by a couple of new devs to sell copies to kids and adults who are into crocodiles or to players who thought they’d get some sort of animal like experience through the title. It’s simplistic in nature but the controls make it a lot more challenging than it has to be. Not much else to say about this title, it’s a 3.5/10 due to the humor factor stated above, But once that novelty wears off you’re left with a shallow, boring, repetitive, ugly game that you’ll probably never play again, you can safely skip this one. title: Some flaws/glitches....  but XBox 360 controller works quite well
text:
UPDTAE: I was getting a horrible clicking sound from the DVD drive when this disc first started up. I upgraded the firmware and the clicking sound went away.

*****

I had a hard time finding online a review/statement that said if the XBox 360 controller hooked up to the PC would work well with this game: it does. I still have to use 'z' for prone and 'j' for drop weapon, but just about everything else can be found on the controller. And before they say it: YES, most hardcore gamers could/do use the keyboard and perform certain functions faster than the XBox controller.

I did, however, find that flying the VTOL was much more responsive and easier with the keyboard.

Walking is slow, and sprinting is the equivalent of what walking should be. A hack for this and other traits is possible.

A lot of effort was put into the environment and the little things you tend to find here and there. I didn't find it too repetitive or blocky, though others may disagree.

More effort should have put into the the hit points and hit areas for the enemy. What I found:
- head shots do not always kill an enemy (aside from the sniper rifle),
- some enemy can take up to three or four clips of ammo to bring down, whereas the guy next to him goes down with a shot to the chest. Those that wear a beret or camo head gear take more shots to bring down, sometimes up to a dozen head shots,
- shooting the back of the head is nowhere near as effective as the face,

There is also some missing AI when it comes to you slowly walking up to a group of enemy in the pitch dark: they always see you coming, even if their back is turned. Not very realistic. You have to prone-crawl your way up to them in order to hide, or use the cloak. Basically, you could be 100 yards from the enemy in near-total darkness and they always have a bead on you, even if you are in heavy brush or behind a rock.

You could be prone in the middle of a wide dirt path in daylight and they would walk right by you.

The vehicles are nerfed quite a bit. Keyboard is easier to maneuver them. Better vehicle controls in Halo 1+2 with the controller than in this game.

The helicopters are way more durable than they need to be. An rpg can demolish a building, but do nothing to a helo? It takes two shoulder rockets to bring down a helo, and a glancing blow does not count, it has to be dead on. In one part, the doors open on a helo and you can launch a rifle grenade or throw one inside it and that will do the trick, but shooting a grenade at the underside does nothing.

The jellyfish-looking alien things are kind of lame, enough said there.

BLOCKING INTERNET REQUESTS:
Yes, you can block the game from connecting with EA and nothing will happen to your game. I use AVG, and have chosen to permanently block the game's request to access EA -- no problems with the game. I say this because some have written that you have to have an Internet connection to use the game... not so.

So, a lot has been put into the environment of the game, but some realistic interaction could be improved upon.
